---
title: "Probability and Distributions"
---

## Why probability comes first {#sec-prob-intro}

Every claim made in an indirect treatment comparison is, at bottom, a claim about a probability
distribution. When we say that the effect of a drug measured in one trial population also describes
what would happen in a different population, we are asserting a relationship between two joint
distributions of covariates and outcomes. When we say that a weighted average of patient-level
predictions reproduces a population mean, we are computing an expectation. When we warn that a
marginal odds ratio from one population does not transport to another, we are invoking a property of
nonlinear transformations of expectations. None of these statements can be made precise, let alone
proved, without the language of measure-theoretic probability. This chapter builds that language from
the ground up.

Three tools recur so often in later chapters that they deserve to be flagged at the outset. The first
is the *expectation operator* together with its conditional version and the *tower property*; almost
every identification and adjustment result in the book is, in its skeleton, an application of the
identity $\mathbb{E}[Y]=\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]]$. The second is *Jensen's inequality*, which is
the reason a nonlinear function of an average differs from the average of the nonlinear function; this
single fact is the source of aggregation bias in meta-regression, of the non-collapsibility of the odds
ratio and the hazard ratio, and of the scale mismatches that make marginal effects hard to transport.
The third is the *multivariate normal distribution*, which is both the exact sampling model behind the
normal-theory likelihoods used throughout network meta-analysis and the approximate model that the
delta method and the central limit theorem deliver for almost any estimator. We develop all three here,
with full proofs.

We follow the measure-theoretic framework of Kolmogorov. Readers with graduate probability may skim to
the boxed statements, but should read @thm-jensen, @thm-cauchy-schwarz-exp, and the multivariate normal
results @thm-mvn-linear and @thm-mvn-conditional in full, since later chapters cite specific steps of
those proofs. The causal motivation throughout is drawn from @hernan2020whatif; the measure theory is
standard and we cite @billingsley1995 and @williams1991 for the results we use without proof. The
material of this chapter corresponds to results A.1 through A.10 of the proof catalogue.

A reader new to measure theory should not try to absorb every proof on a first pass. Read the motivating
prose, the definitions, the *reader translation* that follows each definition, and the *why this matters*
note that follows each major theorem; treat the heaviest proofs, the graphoid axioms
@thm-graphoid-axioms and the differentiation of the moment generating function @thm-mgf-moments, as
optional on a first reading and return to them once the running example below feels familiar. The symbols
used here are collected in the [Notation](/notation.qmd) chapter.

## A running clinical-trial example {#sec-prob-running-example}

Every abstract object in this chapter is a precise way of talking about a concrete quantity in a trial.
To keep that concreteness in view, we fix one small example now and return to it at each transition.

::: {#exm-toy-trial}
## A toy two-arm trial
A randomized trial compares an active drug ($T=1$) against control ($T=0$). Each enrolled patient has a
**baseline severity** $X\in\{0,1\}$, with $0$ meaning low risk and $1$ meaning high risk, and a binary
**response** $Y\in\{0,1\}$, with $1$ meaning the patient responded. A second trial of the same drug, run
in a sicker population, is labeled by a **study indicator** $S\in\{1,2\}$. Suppose the response risks
within each severity stratum are those in the table.

| severity $X$ | share of patients | risk under control $P(Y=1\mid X,T=0)$ | risk under active $P(Y=1\mid X,T=1)$ |
|:---|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| low ($X=0$)  | $0.6$ | $0.20$ | $0.50$ |
| high ($X=1$) | $0.4$ | $0.50$ | $0.90$ |

These numbers are all we need. We will use them to read off a probability space (@sec-prob-space), random
variables and their laws (@sec-random-variables), an expectation (@sec-expectation), a conditional
expectation and the tower property (@sec-conditional), independence and conditional independence
(@sec-independence), and the Jensen gap behind non-collapsibility (@sec-jensen). The potential-outcome
symbols $Y(0),Y(1)$ and the formal treatment-effect machinery are built in Chapter 9; here they serve
only as motivation.
:::

**Two probability spaces, not one.** It is worth deciding at the outset what "an outcome" is, because the
indirect-comparison literature quietly uses two different choices. In a *patient-level* probability space,
one outcome $\omega$ is one patient's full record $(X,T,Y)$, and an event is a set of patients, for
example "high-risk patients who responded." In a *study-level* probability space, one outcome is an
entire trial dataset or its aggregate summary, and an event is a set of possible datasets, for example
"trials in which the observed response rate exceeds $0.5$." Both are legitimate; the table above lives in
the patient-level space, while a sampling statement about an estimated response rate lives in the
study-level space. Whenever the distinction matters we name the space explicitly.

The next table is a field guide to the measure-theoretic vocabulary that follows. Skim it now and refer
back as each term appears; none of it needs to be memorized in advance.

| term | plain meaning | in the trial |
|:---|:---|:---|
| outcome $\omega$ | one elementary result the randomness can produce | one patient's record $(X,T,Y)$ |
| event | a yes-or-no question about $\omega$, formally a set of outcomes | "high risk and responded" |
| $\sigma$-algebra $\mathcal{F}$ | the collection of events we are allowed to ask about | all questions decidable from $(X,T,Y)$ |
| measurable | a map whose preimages of events are events, so probabilities transfer | "response status" as a function of $\omega$ |
| Borel set | a subset of $\mathbb{R}^d$ built from open sets by countable operations | a range of survival times $(0,5]$ |
| disjoint union $\bigsqcup$ | a union of sets no two of which overlap | "responded" and "did not respond" |
| almost surely (a.s.) | with probability one, ignoring a set of probability zero | "every enrolled patient has a severity" |
| $L^1$ | random variables with finite mean, $\mathbb{E}\lvert X\rvert<\infty$ | a finite average response |
| $L^2$ | random variables with finite variance, $\mathbb{E}[X^2]<\infty$ | a finite response variance |
| law / distribution $P_X$ | the probabilities $X$ assigns to value-sets, forgetting $\omega$ | $P(X=1)=0.4$ |
| $\sigma(X)$ | the information in $X$: all events decidable from the value of $X$ | "all we learn once severity is known" |
| version | one specific random variable among several agreeing almost surely | one chosen formula for $\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]$ |

## Probability spaces and $\sigma$-algebras {#sec-prob-space}

The starting point is a triple that encodes a source of randomness, the collection of questions we are
allowed to ask of it, and the answer to each question expressed as a probability.

::: {#def-probability-space}
## Probability space
A **probability space** is a triple $(\Omega,\mathcal{F},P)$ in which:

1. $\Omega$ is a nonempty set, the **sample space**, whose elements $\omega$ are **outcomes**;
2. $\mathcal{F}\subseteq 2^{\Omega}$ is a **$\sigma$-algebra** on $\Omega$, meaning that
   (i) $\Omega\in\mathcal{F}$; (ii) $A\in\mathcal{F}\Rightarrow A^{c}:=\Omega\setminus A\in\mathcal{F}$;
   and (iii) for every sequence $\{A_n\}_{n\ge 1}\subseteq\mathcal{F}$, $\bigcup_{n\ge 1}A_n\in\mathcal{F}$.
   The elements of $\mathcal{F}$ are called **events**;
3. $P:\mathcal{F}\to[0,1]$ is a **probability measure**: $P(\Omega)=1$, and for every sequence of
   pairwise disjoint events $\{A_n\}_{n\ge 1}\subseteq\mathcal{F}$,
   $$
   P\!\left(\bigsqcup_{n\ge 1}A_n\right)=\sum_{n\ge 1}P(A_n).
   $$ {#eq-countable-additivity}
   The property @eq-countable-additivity is called **countable additivity**.
:::

::: {.remark}
**Reader translation.** A probability space is the trial bookkeeping made exact: $\Omega$ is the list of
things that can happen (one entry per patient, in the patient-level reading of @exm-toy-trial),
$\mathcal{F}$ is the list of questions we are allowed to ask, and $P$ assigns each question a number
between $0$ and $1$. The disjoint-union symbol $\bigsqcup$ in @eq-countable-additivity is an ordinary
union with a reminder attached: the events do not overlap, so their probabilities simply add.
:::

In a clinical-trial reading of the definition, an outcome $\omega$ is the entire record of one patient:
baseline covariates, assigned treatment, and follow-up response. The event "the patient survives beyond
five years" is a subset of $\Omega$; if it lies in $\mathcal{F}$ we may speak of its probability. The
requirement that $\mathcal{F}$ be closed under *countable* unions, not merely finite ones, is exactly
what separates a $\sigma$-algebra from a mere algebra of sets, and it is what makes limiting operations,
on which all of analysis depends, available inside the theory. A concrete instance: the event "the
patient relapses at some point during follow-up" is the union over all times $n=1,2,\dots$ of the events
"relapses by time $n$," a genuinely countable union; without closure under such unions we could not even
assign it a probability.

The defining axioms list only a few closure properties. The remaining ones we need follow from them.

::: {#lem-sigma-algebra-closure}
## Closure properties of a $\sigma$-algebra
Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a $\sigma$-algebra on $\Omega$ and $\{A_n\}_{n\ge 1}\subseteq\mathcal{F}$. Then
$\varnothing\in\mathcal{F}$, and $\mathcal{F}$ is closed under countable intersections
$\bigcap_n A_n$, under finite differences $A\setminus B$, and under the set limits
$\limsup_n A_n:=\bigcap_{m\ge 1}\bigcup_{n\ge m}A_n$ and
$\liminf_n A_n:=\bigcup_{m\ge 1}\bigcap_{n\ge m}A_n$.
:::

::: {.remark}
**Reader translation.** The two set limits read as tail events. The expression $\bigcap_{m\ge 1}\bigcup_{n\ge m}A_n$
unpacks as "for every starting time $m$, at least one $A_n$ with $n\ge m$ occurs," which is exactly the
event that $A_n$ occurs for *infinitely many* $n$; this is $\limsup_n A_n$. Dually, $\liminf_n A_n$ is the
event that $A_n$ occurs for *all but finitely many* $n$. The lemma simply says a $\sigma$-algebra is
closed under all the everyday set operations, so every such event has a probability; @exr-borel-cantelli
puts this to work.
:::

::: {.proof}
Since $\Omega\in\mathcal{F}$, axiom (ii) gives $\varnothing=\Omega^{c}\in\mathcal{F}$. For countable
intersections, axiom (ii) gives $A_n^{c}\in\mathcal{F}$, axiom (iii) gives
$\bigcup_n A_n^{c}\in\mathcal{F}$, and axiom (ii) once more gives
$\bigl(\bigcup_n A_n^{c}\bigr)^{c}=\bigcap_n A_n\in\mathcal{F}$ by De Morgan's law (the complement of a
union is the intersection of the complements). For finite
differences, $A\setminus B=A\cap B^{c}$ is the intersection of two events. For the set limits,
$\bigcup_{n\ge m}A_n\in\mathcal{F}$ for each $m$ by axiom (iii), and the countable intersection over $m$
lies in $\mathcal{F}$ by what we have just shown; the argument for $\liminf$ is the mirror image.
$\square$
:::

This is result A.1 of the proof catalogue. We will not construct probability measures by hand. The
existence of measures with prescribed values on a generating class, in particular Lebesgue measure on
$\mathbb{R}$ and the measures induced by distribution functions, is guaranteed by the Carathéodory
extension theorem; see @billingsley1995, §3. We take that machinery as given.

## Random variables and their distributions {#sec-random-variables}

A probability space is rarely interesting on its own. What we observe are numerical summaries of an
outcome: a covariate, a treatment indicator, a survival time. These are functions on $\Omega$, and to
assign probabilities to statements about their values we require that the preimage of every reasonable
set of values be an event.

Throughout, $\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$ denotes the **Borel $\sigma$-algebra** on $\mathbb{R}^{d}$,
the smallest $\sigma$-algebra containing all open sets. Its existence follows from the fact that an
arbitrary intersection of $\sigma$-algebras is again a $\sigma$-algebra, so one may intersect all
$\sigma$-algebras containing the open sets.

::: {#def-random-variable}
## Random variable and its law
Let $(\Omega,\mathcal{F},P)$ be a probability space and $(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{S}')$ a **measurable space**
(a set $\mathcal{S}$ paired with a $\sigma$-algebra $\mathcal{S}'$ of its subsets; the prime is merely a
label distinguishing the $\sigma$-algebra from the set, not a derivative).
A function $X:\Omega\to\mathcal{S}$ is **measurable**, and is called a **random variable** when
$(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{S}')=(\mathbb{R},\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}))$ and a **random vector** when
$(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{S}')=(\mathbb{R}^{d},\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^{d}))$, if
$$
X^{-1}(B):=\{\omega\in\Omega: X(\omega)\in B\}\in\mathcal{F}\qquad\text{for every }B\in\mathcal{S}'.
$$
The **law** (or **distribution**) of $X$ is the set function $P_X$ on $(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{S}')$
defined by the **pushforward**
$$
P_X(B):=P\bigl(X^{-1}(B)\bigr),\qquad B\in\mathcal{S}'.
$$ {#eq-pushforward}
:::

::: {.remark}
**Reader translation.** A random variable is a measurement: it reads a number off each outcome.
Measurability is the modest demand that every question about that number ("is severity high?", "is the
response time under five years?") be a legitimate event, so it has a probability. The **law** $P_X$ is
what remains after forgetting the patient and keeping only how often $X$ lands in each value-set; the
**pushforward** @eq-pushforward is the recipe for it, pushing each value-set $B$ back through $X$ to a
patient event $X^{-1}(B)$ and taking its probability. From the change-of-variables identity
@eq-change-of-variables onward we work entirely with the law and never mention $\Omega$ again.
:::

::: {#prp-law-is-measure}
## The law is a probability measure
For a random variable $X$, the pushforward $P_X$ of @eq-pushforward is a probability measure on
$(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{S}')$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Measurability of $X$ guarantees $X^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal{F}$, so $P_X(B)$ is defined. First,
$P_X(\mathcal{S})=P(X^{-1}(\mathcal{S}))=P(\Omega)=1$, because every $\omega$ is mapped somewhere.
Nonnegativity is inherited from $P$. For countable additivity, let $\{B_n\}$ be pairwise disjoint in
$\mathcal{S}'$. Preimages preserve disjointness and distribute over unions,
$X^{-1}\bigl(\bigsqcup_n B_n\bigr)=\bigsqcup_n X^{-1}(B_n)$, so by countable additivity of $P$,
$$
P_X\!\left(\bigsqcup_n B_n\right)
=P\!\left(\bigsqcup_n X^{-1}(B_n)\right)
=\sum_n P\bigl(X^{-1}(B_n)\bigr)
=\sum_n P_X(B_n).\qquad\square
$$
:::

This is result A.2. The law $P_X$ is the object we actually reason about; the underlying $\Omega$
recedes into the background. A random variable $X$ on $\mathbb{R}$ is summarized by its **cumulative
distribution function** (CDF)
$$
F_X(x):=P_X\bigl((-\infty,x]\bigr)=P(X\le x),\qquad x\in\mathbb{R}.
$$
Every CDF is nondecreasing, right-continuous, and satisfies $F_X(-\infty)=0$, $F_X(+\infty)=1$, and
conversely every function with these properties is the CDF of a unique law on
$(\mathbb{R},\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}))$; see @billingsley1995, §14. We write $F_X^{-1}$ for the
generalized inverse (quantile function) $F_X^{-1}(u)=\inf\{x:F_X(x)\ge u\}$, the value below which a
fraction $u$ of the distribution lies, the population version of a sample quantile; it returns in Part V
to generate correlated covariates by the inverse-CDF method. The standard normal CDF and
density are written $\Phi$ and $\phi$ throughout, following the notation chapter.

The practical dividend of the pushforward is the **change-of-variables identity** for expectations,
which lets us integrate over the values of $X$ rather than over $\Omega$:
$$
\mathbb{E}[h(X)]=\int_{\Omega}h(X(\omega))\,dP(\omega)=\int_{\mathcal{S}}h(s)\,dP_X(s),
$$ {#eq-change-of-variables}
valid for every measurable $h$ for which either side is defined. In words, to average any function of $X$
we integrate over the *values* of $X$ weighted by its law $P_X$; the abstract sample space has done its
job and disappears, which is why every later computation is phrased in terms of laws and densities rather
than $\Omega$.

The words introduced so far are easy to conflate. They line up as follows.

| object | what it is | type | trial reading |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| event | a set of outcomes | subset of $\Omega$ | "high risk and responded" |
| random variable $X$ | a measurement on outcomes | function $\Omega\to\mathbb{R}$ | severity, treatment, or response |
| law / distribution $P_X$ | how often $X$ hits each value-set | measure on $\mathbb{R}$ | $P(X=1)=0.4$ |
| CDF $F_X$ | the law accumulated up to $x$ | function $\mathbb{R}\to[0,1]$ | $F_X(0)=P(X\le 0)=0.6$ |
| density / mass $f_X$ | the law per unit value | function on $\mathbb{R}$ | $f_X(1)=0.4,\ f_X(0)=0.6$ |
| expectation $\mathbb{E}[X]$ | the law's center of mass | a single number | mean severity $\mathbb{E}[X]=0.4$ |

The first three describe *where the randomness lives*; the last three are *summaries* of the law. A
density exists only when the law is smooth enough (the continuous case) or sits on isolated points (the
discrete case, where it is a mass function), but the CDF and the expectation always exist. We prove the
meaning of these integrals next.

## Expectation as an integral {#sec-expectation}

The **expectation** of a random variable $X$ is its Lebesgue integral against $P$,
$\mathbb{E}[X]:=\int_{\Omega}X\,dP$, defined in the usual three stages. For a nonnegative **simple**
random variable $X=\sum_{k=1}^{m}c_k\mathbf{1}_{A_k}$ with $c_k\ge 0$ and $A_k\in\mathcal{F}$ (here the
**indicator** $\mathbf{1}_{A}$ equals $1$ on the event $A$ and $0$ off it; we also write
$\mathbf{1}\{X=x\}$ for the indicator of the event $\{X=x\}$), one sets
$\mathbb{E}[X]=\sum_{k=1}^{m}c_k P(A_k)$. For a general nonnegative measurable $X$, one sets
$\mathbb{E}[X]=\sup\{\mathbb{E}[S]: 0\le S\le X,\ S\text{ simple}\}\in[0,\infty]$. For a general $X$, one
writes $X=X^{+}-X^{-}$ with $X^{\pm}=\max(\pm X,0)$ and sets
$\mathbb{E}[X]=\mathbb{E}[X^{+}]-\mathbb{E}[X^{-}]$ whenever at least one term is finite; $X$ is
**integrable**, written $X\in L^1$ (the space of integrable random variables), when
$\mathbb{E}|X|<\infty$. The construction and the elementary
properties (monotonicity, and additivity on simple functions) are standard; see @billingsley1995, §15.

::: {.remark}
**Reader translation.** Expectation is a weighted average, and the three-stage construction only makes
that idea survive when the averaging has infinitely many pieces. For a discrete measurement it is the
familiar sum $\sum_x x\,P(X=x)$: in @exm-toy-trial the severity $X$ is $\mathrm{Ber}(0.4)$, so
$\mathbb{E}[X]=0\cdot 0.6+1\cdot 0.4=0.4$. For a continuous measurement the sum becomes the integral
$\int x\,f_X(x)\,dx$. The simple-then-nonnegative-then-general staircase is precisely what guarantees
these are one notion, so the single symbol $\mathbb{E}$ covers a finite trial average, a discrete mean,
and a continuous integral without contradiction, and continues to work for unbounded outcomes.
:::

Two limit theorems govern the interchange of limits with integration and are cited, not reproved, here;
they are the analytic backbone of every later argument that passes a limit inside an expectation. They
constitute result A.3.

::: {#thm-monotone-convergence}
## Monotone convergence (cited)
If $0\le X_n\uparrow X$ almost surely (the arrow $\uparrow$ denotes that $X_n$ increases to its limit, and
**almost surely**, abbreviated a.s., means with probability one, that is, outside a set of outcomes of
probability zero), that is, $X_n(\omega)$ is nondecreasing in $n$ with limit
$X(\omega)$ for $P$-almost every $\omega$, then $\mathbb{E}[X_n]\uparrow\mathbb{E}[X]$.
:::

::: {#thm-dominated-convergence}
## Dominated convergence (cited)
If $X_n\to X$ almost surely and there is an integrable $Y$ with $|X_n|\le Y$ almost surely for all $n$,
then $X$ is integrable and $\mathbb{E}[X_n]\to\mathbb{E}[X]$; moreover $\mathbb{E}|X_n-X|\to 0$.
:::

Proofs are in @billingsley1995, §16, the second deduced from Fatou's lemma. We will reference these as
@thm-monotone-convergence and @thm-dominated-convergence. The first result we prove from scratch is the
linearity of expectation, the most heavily used identity in the book.

::: {#thm-expectation-linearity}
## Linearity of expectation
Let $X,Y\in L^1$ and $a,b\in\mathbb{R}$. Then $aX+bY\in L^1$ and
$$
\mathbb{E}[aX+bY]=a\,\mathbb{E}[X]+b\,\mathbb{E}[Y].
$$
:::

::: {.proof}
Integrability of $aX+bY$ follows from the triangle inequality $|aX+bY|\le|a|\,|X|+|b|\,|Y|$ and
monotonicity of the integral. For the identity we proceed through the construction. For nonnegative
simple functions $S=\sum_k c_k\mathbf{1}_{A_k}$ and $T=\sum_\ell d_\ell\mathbf{1}_{B_\ell}$, refining to
the common partition generated by $\{A_k\}$ and $\{B_\ell\}$ shows
$\mathbb{E}[\alpha S+\beta T]=\alpha\,\mathbb{E}[S]+\beta\,\mathbb{E}[T]$ for $\alpha,\beta\ge 0$, since
on each atom of the refinement the integrand is a constant and $P$ is additive over the atoms. For
nonnegative measurable $X,Y$, take simple $0\le S_n\uparrow X$ and $0\le T_n\uparrow Y$ (such sequences
exist by the standard dyadic approximation: round $X$ down to the nearest multiple of $2^{-n}$ and cap at
height $n$, giving simple functions that increase pointwise to $X$). Then $\alpha S_n+\beta T_n\uparrow \alpha X+\beta Y$, and
@thm-monotone-convergence gives
$$
\mathbb{E}[\alpha X+\beta Y]=\lim_n\mathbb{E}[\alpha S_n+\beta T_n]
=\alpha\lim_n\mathbb{E}[S_n]+\beta\lim_n\mathbb{E}[T_n]=\alpha\,\mathbb{E}[X]+\beta\,\mathbb{E}[Y]
$$
for $\alpha,\beta\ge 0$. Finally, for general integrable $X,Y$ and real $a,b$, decompose each variable
into positive and negative parts and each coefficient into sign and magnitude, and combine the
nonnegative case with the additive splitting $\mathbb{E}[Z]=\mathbb{E}[Z^{+}]-\mathbb{E}[Z^{-}]$; every
term is finite by integrability, so the rearrangement is legitimate. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Why this matters.** Linearity is the workhorse behind every weighted estimator in the book. An inverse
probability weighted mean, a matching-adjusted average, and a network meta-analysis contrast are all
linear combinations of responses, and linearity is what lets us pass expectations through them. We prove
it from the construction, rather than assume it, because the unbiasedness arguments of Part IV and the
limit theorems we later cite all rest on this identity holding exactly, not approximately.
:::

Linearity is half of result A.4; the tower property is the other half and is proved in
@sec-conditional after we have conditional expectation in hand. We also record the second-moment
summaries that organize all variance calculations to come.

::: {#def-variance-covariance}
## Variance, covariance, and the covariance matrix
For $X,Y\in L^2$, that is, $\mathbb{E}[X^2]<\infty$ and $\mathbb{E}[Y^2]<\infty$, define
$$
\mathrm{Var}(X):=\mathbb{E}\bigl[(X-\mathbb{E}X)^2\bigr],\qquad
\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb{E}\bigl[(X-\mathbb{E}X)(Y-\mathbb{E}Y)\bigr].
$$
For a random vector $\mathbf{X}=(X_1,\dots,X_p)^{\top}$ with each $X_i\in L^2$ and mean
$\boldsymbol{\mu}=\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{X}]$ (taken componentwise), the **covariance matrix** is the
$p\times p$ matrix
$$
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}:=\mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf{X})
:=\mathbb{E}\bigl[(\mathbf{X}-\boldsymbol{\mu})(\mathbf{X}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^{\top}\bigr],
\qquad \Sigma_{ij}=\mathrm{Cov}(X_i,X_j).
$$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Reader translation.** Variance is the average squared distance of a measurement from its mean, a single
number for spread; covariance is the signed version for a pair, positive when the two move together. The
covariance matrix $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ packages all pairwise covariances of a random vector, and the
identity @eq-var-quadratic-form below says the spread of any linear summary $\mathbf{a}^{\top}\mathbf{X}$
is read off $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ as a quadratic form. This is the hinge between probability and the
matrix algebra of Chapter 3.
:::

By linearity, $\mathrm{Var}(X)=\mathbb{E}[X^2]-(\mathbb{E}X)^2$ and $\mathrm{Cov}$ is symmetric and
bilinear. A computation we will reuse: for a fixed vector $\mathbf{a}\in\mathbb{R}^p$,
$$
\mathrm{Var}(\mathbf{a}^{\top}\mathbf{X})
=\mathbb{E}\bigl[(\mathbf{a}^{\top}(\mathbf{X}-\boldsymbol{\mu}))^2\bigr]
=\mathbf{a}^{\top}\,\mathbb{E}\bigl[(\mathbf{X}-\boldsymbol{\mu})(\mathbf{X}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^{\top}\bigr]\,\mathbf{a}
=\mathbf{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\,\mathbf{a},
$$ {#eq-var-quadratic-form}
which expresses the variance of a linear combination as a quadratic form in the covariance matrix. This
identity is the bridge to @sec-cov-psd.

## Conditional expectation and the tower property {#sec-conditional}

For a discrete random variable $X$ with $P(X=x)>0$ one defines the conditional expectation
$\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X=x]$ as the ratio $\mathbb{E}[Y\mathbf{1}\{X=x\}]/P(X=x)$, the average response among
the patients with $X=x$. This is the everyday notion of a subgroup mean. The difficulty is that for a
*continuous* $X$ every single value has probability zero, $P(X=x)=0$, so the ratio becomes the
meaningless $0/0$ and the elementary definition collapses. The measure-theoretic definition repairs this
not by rescuing the ratio but by characterizing the whole function $x\mapsto\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X=x]$ at
once, through an averaging identity that never evaluates a probability-zero event. It reduces to the
familiar subgroup mean whenever the subgroups have positive probability, as we verify in
@exm-cond-exp-strata below.

::: {#def-conditional-expectation}
## Conditional expectation
Let $Y\in L^1$ on $(\Omega,\mathcal{F},P)$ and let $\mathcal{G}\subseteq\mathcal{F}$ be a
sub-$\sigma$-algebra. A **conditional expectation** of $Y$ given $\mathcal{G}$ is any
$\mathcal{G}$-measurable random variable $Z$ with $Z\in L^1$ satisfying the **defining property**
$$
\mathbb{E}[Z\,\mathbf{1}_A]=\mathbb{E}[Y\,\mathbf{1}_A]\qquad\text{for all }A\in\mathcal{G}.
$$ {#eq-cond-exp-defining}
Any two such $Z$ agree almost surely; we fix one version and write $Z=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid\mathcal{G}]$. When
$\mathcal{G}=\sigma(X)$ is the $\sigma$-algebra generated by a random variable or vector $X$, we write
$\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]$, and there is a measurable function $m$ with $\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]=m(X)$ almost
surely; the value $m(x)$ is what we mean by $\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X=x]$.
:::

::: {.remark}
**Reader translation.** Think of $\mathcal{G}$ as the information you are allowed to use, and
$\mathbb{E}[Y\mid\mathcal{G}]$ as your best guess of $Y$ given only that information. The defining
property @eq-cond-exp-defining says the guess must get the totals right: on every event $A$ you are
allowed to see, the guess and the truth average to the same thing. Two guesses that always agree on those
events agree almost surely, which is why we speak of *a* version and then fix one. When the information is
"the value of $X$," written $\mathcal{G}=\sigma(X)$, the guess is a function of $X$ and its value at $x$
is the subgroup mean $\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X=x]$. Two sanity checks: $\mathbb{E}[Y\mid\mathcal{G}]=Y$ when $Y$
is itself $\mathcal{G}$-measurable (you already know $Y$), and $\mathbb{E}[Y\mid\mathcal{G}]$ is the
constant $\mathbb{E}[Y]$ when $\mathcal{G}$ carries no information about $Y$.
:::

The existence of a random variable satisfying @eq-cond-exp-defining is guaranteed by a deep theorem of
measure theory, the **Radon-Nikodym theorem**. We record the construction for completeness and then never
use its internals again; a reader meeting these words for the first time may take existence on faith and
lose nothing that follows. Concretely, the set function
$\nu(A):=\mathbb{E}[Y\,\mathbf{1}_A]$ for $A\in\mathcal{G}$ is a finite signed measure on
$(\Omega,\mathcal{G})$, absolutely continuous with respect to the restriction $P|_{\mathcal{G}}$, so it
has a $\mathcal{G}$-measurable density $Z=d\nu/dP|_{\mathcal{G}}$, which is @eq-cond-exp-defining; see
@williams1991, §9. Uniqueness up to null sets is immediate: if $Z,Z'$ both satisfy
@eq-cond-exp-defining, then $\mathbb{E}[(Z-Z')\mathbf{1}_A]=0$ for all $A\in\mathcal{G}$; taking
$A=\{Z-Z'>0\}\in\mathcal{G}$ forces $P(Z-Z'>0)=0$, and likewise for the reverse inequality. This is
result A.5. We record the operational properties; the tower property is the one we own and prove in
full.

The definition earns its keep by reducing to the elementary subgroup mean. We check this on the running
trial, and read off the tower property it will satisfy.

::: {#exm-cond-exp-strata}
## Subgroup means in the toy trial
Work on the control arm of @exm-toy-trial, where severity $X$ has $P(X=0)=0.6$ and $P(X=1)=0.4$ and the
response risks are $\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X=0]=0.20$ and $\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X=1]=0.50$. Take
$\mathcal{G}=\sigma(X)$.

*The elementary ratio.* Since $X$ is discrete with positive cell probabilities,
$$
\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X=1]=\frac{\mathbb{E}[Y\,\mathbf{1}\{X=1\}]}{P(X=1)}=\frac{P(Y=1,\,X=1)}{P(X=1)}
=\frac{0.4\cdot 0.50}{0.4}=0.50,
$$
and likewise $\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X=0]=0.20$. So $\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]=m(X)$ with $m(0)=0.20$ and $m(1)=0.50$.

*The defining property.* This same $m(X)$ satisfies @eq-cond-exp-defining. The nontrivial events of
$\sigma(X)$ are $\{X=0\}$, $\{X=1\}$, and their union $\Omega$; on $A=\{X=1\}$,
$$
\mathbb{E}[m(X)\,\mathbf{1}_A]=0.50\cdot P(X=1)=0.50\cdot 0.4=0.20=\mathbb{E}[Y\,\mathbf{1}_A],
$$
and similarly on $\{X=0\}$, so the measure-theoretic guess and the elementary subgroup mean coincide.

*The tower property in advance.* Averaging the subgroup means against the subgroup sizes recovers the
overall mean,
$$
\mathbb{E}[Y]=0.6\cdot 0.20+0.4\cdot 0.50=0.12+0.20=0.32,
$$
which is the law of total expectation $\mathbb{E}[Y]=\mathbb{E}\bigl[\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]\bigr]$. This
"average the subgroup means and recover the whole" is the identity @thm-tower-property now proves in
general.
:::

::: {#thm-tower-property}
## Tower property
Let $Y\in L^1$ and let $\mathcal{H}\subseteq\mathcal{G}\subseteq\mathcal{F}$ be nested
sub-$\sigma$-algebras. Then $\mathbb{E}[Y\mid\mathcal{G}]\in L^1$ and
$$
\mathbb{E}\bigl[\,\mathbb{E}[Y\mid\mathcal{G}]\,\big|\,\mathcal{H}\,\bigr]=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid\mathcal{H}]
\quad\text{a.s.};
$$ {#eq-tower}
in particular, taking $\mathcal{H}=\{\varnothing,\Omega\}$ the trivial $\sigma$-algebra,
$$
\mathbb{E}\bigl[\,\mathbb{E}[Y\mid\mathcal{G}]\,\bigr]=\mathbb{E}[Y].
$$ {#eq-tower-mean}
:::

::: {.proof}
Write $Z=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid\mathcal{G}]$. Integrability of $Z$: applying @eq-cond-exp-defining with the
events $A^{+}=\{Z>0\}$ and $A^{-}=\{Z\le 0\}$, both in $\mathcal{G}$, gives
$\mathbb{E}|Z|=\mathbb{E}[Z\mathbf{1}_{A^{+}}]-\mathbb{E}[Z\mathbf{1}_{A^{-}}]
=\mathbb{E}[Y\mathbf{1}_{A^{+}}]-\mathbb{E}[Y\mathbf{1}_{A^{-}}]\le\mathbb{E}|Y|<\infty$, so $Z\in L^1$.

Let $W=\mathbb{E}[Z\mid\mathcal{H}]$, which is $\mathcal{H}$-measurable by construction. To show
$W=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid\mathcal{H}]$ it suffices, by uniqueness in @def-conditional-expectation, to verify
the defining property $\mathbb{E}[W\mathbf{1}_A]=\mathbb{E}[Y\mathbf{1}_A]$ for every
$A\in\mathcal{H}$. Fix such an $A$. Since $W=\mathbb{E}[Z\mid\mathcal{H}]$ and $A\in\mathcal{H}$, the
defining property of $W$ gives $\mathbb{E}[W\mathbf{1}_A]=\mathbb{E}[Z\mathbf{1}_A]$. Since
$A\in\mathcal{H}\subseteq\mathcal{G}$, the defining property of $Z=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid\mathcal{G}]$ gives
$\mathbb{E}[Z\mathbf{1}_A]=\mathbb{E}[Y\mathbf{1}_A]$. Chaining the two equalities yields
$\mathbb{E}[W\mathbf{1}_A]=\mathbb{E}[Y\mathbf{1}_A]$, which is @eq-tower. Specializing to the trivial
$\mathcal{H}$, whose only events are $\varnothing$ and $\Omega$, the random variable
$\mathbb{E}[Y\mid\mathcal{H}]$ is the constant $\mathbb{E}[Y]$, and @eq-tower-mean follows by taking
expectations on both sides of @eq-tower, that is, by setting $A=\Omega$ in
$\mathbb{E}[Z\mathbf{1}_A]=\mathbb{E}[Y\mathbf{1}_A]$. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Why this matters.** The tower property is the engine of identification. In a trial we can estimate a
*conditional* mean, the response within each covariate stratum; what a decision maker wants is a
*marginal* mean in some target population. The tower property
$\mathbb{E}[Y]=\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]]$ is precisely the bridge: average the stratum-specific
means against the target's covariate distribution and you obtain the target's marginal mean, exactly as
in @exm-cond-exp-strata. Every standardization, transportability, and population-adjustment formula later
in the book, including the core ML-NMR estimand of Part V, is this identity with a particular choice of
distribution to average over.
:::

The tower property completes result A.4. We will use the remaining standard properties of conditional
expectation, proved in @williams1991, §9: linearity; **taking out what is known** (if a factor is already
determined by the conditioning information, it slides outside the conditional expectation as a constant),
namely
$\mathbb{E}[g(X)Y\mid X]=g(X)\,\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]$ for bounded measurable $g$ (for an indicator
$g=\mathbf{1}_B$ with $B\in\sigma(X)$ this is immediate from @eq-cond-exp-defining, and the general case
follows by linearity and @thm-monotone-convergence); and the fact that
$\mathbb{E}[Y\mid\mathcal{G}]=\mathbb{E}[Y]$ when $Y$ is independent of $\mathcal{G}$. Two immediate
corollaries are recorded next.

::: {#cor-total-expectation}
## Law of total expectation and total probability
For $Y\in L^1$ and any sub-$\sigma$-algebra $\mathcal{G}$, $\mathbb{E}[Y]=\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[Y\mid\mathcal{G}]]$.
For an event $B$ and a countable partition $\{A_n\}$ of $\Omega$ into events with $P(A_n)>0$,
$$
P(B)=\sum_n P(B\mid A_n)\,P(A_n),\qquad P(B\mid A_n):=\frac{P(B\cap A_n)}{P(A_n)}.
$$
:::

::: {.proof}
The first claim is @eq-tower-mean. For the second, apply linearity and countable additivity to the
indicator $\mathbf{1}_B=\sum_n\mathbf{1}_{B\cap A_n}$: taking expectations,
$P(B)=\sum_n P(B\cap A_n)=\sum_n P(B\mid A_n)P(A_n)$, the last step by the definition of conditional
probability. Interchanging expectation and the infinite sum of nonnegative terms is licensed by
@thm-monotone-convergence applied to the partial sums. $\square$
:::

This is result A.9. The variance counterpart of the tower property is the decomposition that separates
within-group from between-group variation; we will invoke it for mixed-count likelihoods later.

::: {#cor-total-variance}
## Law of total variance
For $Y\in L^2$ and a random vector $X$,
$$
\mathrm{Var}(Y)=\mathbb{E}\bigl[\mathrm{Var}(Y\mid X)\bigr]+\mathrm{Var}\bigl(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]\bigr),
$$ {#eq-total-variance}
where $\mathrm{Var}(Y\mid X):=\mathbb{E}[(Y-\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X])^2\mid X]$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Write $m(X)=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]$ and decompose $Y-\mathbb{E}Y=(Y-m(X))+(m(X)-\mathbb{E}Y)$. Squaring and
taking expectations,
$$
\mathrm{Var}(Y)=\mathbb{E}[(Y-m(X))^2]+2\,\mathbb{E}[(Y-m(X))(m(X)-\mathbb{E}Y)]+\mathbb{E}[(m(X)-\mathbb{E}Y)^2].
$$
The cross term vanishes: conditioning on $X$ and taking out the $X$-measurable factor $m(X)-\mathbb{E}Y$,
$$
\mathbb{E}[(Y-m(X))(m(X)-\mathbb{E}Y)\mid X]=(m(X)-\mathbb{E}Y)\,\mathbb{E}[Y-m(X)\mid X]
=(m(X)-\mathbb{E}Y)\cdot 0=0,
$$
since $\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]=m(X)$; by @eq-tower-mean the unconditional cross term is then $0$. The first
term equals $\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[(Y-m(X))^2\mid X]]=\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{Var}(Y\mid X)]$ by the tower
property. The third term is $\mathrm{Var}(m(X))=\mathrm{Var}(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X])$ because
$\mathbb{E}[m(X)]=\mathbb{E}Y$. Summing gives @eq-total-variance. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Why this matters.** The law of total variance splits the variability of an outcome into a part *within*
covariate strata and a part *between* them. For a hospital's monthly count of deaths it separates
within-ward chance fluctuation from genuine between-ward differences in patient risk; the mixed-count
likelihoods of Part V use exactly this split to attach the right variance to an aggregate event count,
rather than the too-small variance a single binomial would suggest.
:::

## Independence and conditional independence {#sec-independence}

Independence is the formal statement that knowledge of one variable conveys nothing about another.

::: {#def-independence}
## Independence
Events $A,B\in\mathcal{F}$ are **independent** if $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)$. Random vectors $X$ and $Y$ are
**independent**, written $X\perp Y$, if their joint law is the product of their marginals, equivalently
if
$$
\mathbb{E}[f(X)g(Y)]=\mathbb{E}[f(X)]\,\mathbb{E}[g(Y)]
$$
for all bounded measurable $f,g$. A family $\{X_i\}_{i\in I}$ is **mutually independent** if for every
finite subset the joint law factors into the product of marginals.
:::

::: {.remark}
**Reader translation.** Independence means learning one variable tells you nothing about the other, so
their probabilities multiply. In @exm-toy-trial, if a fair coin assigned treatment regardless of
severity, then $T\perp X$ and $P(T=1,\,X=1)=P(T=1)\,P(X=1)=0.5\cdot 0.4=0.20$. The expectation form
$\mathbb{E}[f(X)g(Y)]=\mathbb{E}[f(X)]\,\mathbb{E}[g(Y)]$ is the same statement read through test
functions: no function of one variable correlates with any function of the other.
:::

Independence implies uncorrelatedness: taking $f,g$ the identity on bounded variables, or passing to the
limit under domination for $L^2$ variables, gives $\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)=0$. The converse fails in general;
@exr-uncorrelated-not-independent supplies a standard counterexample. The conditional version of
independence is the relation on which the entire causal-inference apparatus of Part II rests.

::: {#def-conditional-independence}
## Conditional independence
Random vectors $X$ and $Y$ are **conditionally independent given** $Z$, written $X\perp Y\mid Z$, if for
all bounded measurable $f,g$,
$$
\mathbb{E}[f(X)g(Y)\mid Z]=\mathbb{E}[f(X)\mid Z]\,\mathbb{E}[g(Y)\mid Z]\quad\text{a.s.}
$$ {#eq-cond-indep}
Equivalently, the conditional joint law of $(X,Y)$ given $Z$ factors as the product of the conditional
marginal laws.
:::

::: {.remark}
**Reader translation.** Conditional independence says that *once you know $Z$*, learning $Y$ tells you
nothing more about $X$. This is the language of adjustment. The defining assumption of a covariate-adjusted
trial is that treatment is assigned without regard to the patient's potential outcomes once the
covariates used in assignment are fixed, written $T\perp (Y(0),Y(1))\mid X$ and called *conditional
ignorability* in Chapter 9. Reading $X$ for $Z$, $T$ for one variable, and a potential outcome for the
other, every adjustment method in Part II is an effort to make a statement of exactly this shape hold.
:::

The relation $\cdot\perp\cdot\mid\cdot$ obeys a small algebra of inference rules, the **graphoid
axioms**, which is what allows high-dimensional conditional-independence statements to be manipulated
symbolically; this manipulation is exactly how the propensity-score reduction of Chapter 10 is justified,
starting from the conditional ignorability of Chapter 9.

The five rules below are the algebra of this relation. A first-time reader should take in the
plain-language column of the roadmap, read the causal illustration in @exm-graphoid-binary, and treat the
proof itself as optional; later chapters invoke the rules, not the proof technique.

| axiom | symbolic form | plain meaning | where it is used |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| (G1) symmetry | $X\perp Y\mid Z\iff Y\perp X\mid Z$ | irrelevance is mutual | every manipulation |
| (G2) decomposition | $X\perp(Y,W)\mid Z\Rightarrow X\perp Y\mid Z$ | irrelevant jointly, so irrelevant singly | dropping a nuisance variable |
| (G3) weak union | $X\perp(Y,W)\mid Z\Rightarrow X\perp Y\mid(Z,W)$ | revealing more keeps irrelevance | conditioning on extra covariates |
| (G4) contraction | $X\perp Y\mid Z$ and $X\perp W\mid(Z,Y)\Rightarrow X\perp(Y,W)\mid Z$ | combine two irrelevancies into one | building up an adjustment set |
| (G5) intersection | two crossed irrelevancies $\Rightarrow$ joint irrelevance | holds only with overlap | justified under positivity |

::: {#exm-graphoid-binary}
## Conditional independence on three binary variables
Let $X$ be a covariate, $T$ a treatment, and $Y$ an outcome, all binary, and suppose treatment is
assigned by a coin whose bias depends only on $X$, so $P(T=1\mid X,Y)=e(X)$ with $e(0)=0.3$ and
$e(1)=0.7$. Then $T\perp Y\mid X$, because given $X$ the assignment probability does not look at $Y$:
$P(T=1\mid X,Y)=e(X)=P(T=1\mid X)$. Decomposition (G2) is the statement that if assignment ignores the
*pair* $(Y,W)$ given $X$, where $W$ is, say, a downstream marker, then it ignores $Y$ alone given $X$:
summing the joint factorization over the values of $W$ leaves the same product form. Contraction (G4)
runs the other way: if assignment ignores $Y$ given $X$, and also ignores $W$ given $(X,Y)$, then it
ignores the pair $(Y,W)$ given $X$. These are the moves that let us add or drop variables from an
adjustment set without re-deriving everything, and they are exactly what the propensity-score argument of
Chapter 10 uses.
:::

::: {#thm-graphoid-axioms}
## Graphoid axioms
The conditional-independence relation of @def-conditional-independence satisfies, for all random vectors
$X,Y,Z,W$:

- **(G1) Symmetry:** $X\perp Y\mid Z\iff Y\perp X\mid Z$.
- **(G2) Decomposition:** $X\perp (Y,W)\mid Z\Rightarrow X\perp Y\mid Z$.
- **(G3) Weak union:** $X\perp (Y,W)\mid Z\Rightarrow X\perp Y\mid (Z,W)$.
- **(G4) Contraction:** $\bigl(X\perp Y\mid Z\bigr)\wedge\bigl(X\perp W\mid (Z,Y)\bigr)\Rightarrow X\perp (Y,W)\mid Z$.
- **(G5) Intersection:** if the joint density of $(X,Y,Z,W)$ is strictly positive on its support, then
  $\bigl(X\perp Y\mid (Z,W)\bigr)\wedge\bigl(X\perp W\mid (Z,Y)\bigr)\Rightarrow X\perp (Y,W)\mid Z$.

[machine-checked: `theories/ConditionalIndep.v`, Lemmas `cond_indep_symmetry`,
`cond_indep_decomposition`; Theorems `cond_indep_weak_union`, `cond_indep_contraction`]
:::

::: {.proof}
**(G1)** is immediate, since @eq-cond-indep is symmetric under exchanging the pair $(f,X)$ with $(g,Y)$.

**(G2)** Apply @eq-cond-indep with $g$ depending on the $Y$-coordinate alone, that is, take the test
function on $(Y,W)$ to be $g(Y)\cdot 1$. The hypothesis $X\perp (Y,W)\mid Z$ then reads
$\mathbb{E}[f(X)g(Y)\mid Z]=\mathbb{E}[f(X)\mid Z]\,\mathbb{E}[g(Y)\mid Z]$ for all bounded measurable
$f,g$, which is precisely $X\perp Y\mid Z$.

**(G3)** We must show $\mathbb{E}[f(X)g(Y)\mid Z,W]=\mathbb{E}[f(X)\mid Z,W]\,\mathbb{E}[g(Y)\mid Z,W]$.
The hypothesis $X\perp(Y,W)\mid Z$ gives, for every bounded measurable $f$ and every bounded measurable
$h$ of $(Y,W)$,
$$
\mathbb{E}[f(X)h(Y,W)\mid Z]=\mathbb{E}[f(X)\mid Z]\,\mathbb{E}[h(Y,W)\mid Z].
$$
Taking $h(Y,W)=k(W)$ a function of $W$ alone shows $X\perp W\mid Z$, whence
$\mathbb{E}[f(X)\mid Z,W]=\mathbb{E}[f(X)\mid Z]$ almost surely: indeed, the right side is
$(Z,W)$-measurable, and for any bounded $k$,
$\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[f(X)\mid Z]\,k(W)\mid Z]=\mathbb{E}[f(X)\mid Z]\,\mathbb{E}[k(W)\mid Z]
=\mathbb{E}[f(X)k(W)\mid Z]$, which by the defining property identifies $\mathbb{E}[f(X)\mid Z]$ as a
version of $\mathbb{E}[f(X)\mid Z,W]$. Now taking $h(Y,W)=g(Y)k(W)$ in the displayed identity and using
taking-out-what-is-known on the $W$-measurable factors,
$$
\mathbb{E}\!\left[k(W)\,\mathbb{E}[f(X)g(Y)\mid Z,W]\,\middle|\,Z\right]
=\mathbb{E}\!\left[k(W)\,\mathbb{E}[f(X)\mid Z,W]\,\mathbb{E}[g(Y)\mid Z,W]\,\middle|\,Z\right]
$$
for every bounded $k$, where on the right we substituted
$\mathbb{E}[f(X)\mid Z,W]=\mathbb{E}[f(X)\mid Z]$ and reassembled. Since this holds for all bounded
measurable $k$ of $W$, the two $(Z,W)$-measurable integrands agree almost surely, which is the claim.

**(G4)** Fix bounded measurable $f,g,k$ acting on $X,Y,W$ respectively. By taking out what is known and
the hypothesis $X\perp W\mid (Z,Y)$,
$$
\mathbb{E}[f(X)g(Y)k(W)\mid Z]
=\mathbb{E}\bigl[g(Y)\,\mathbb{E}[f(X)k(W)\mid Z,Y]\,\big|\,Z\bigr]
=\mathbb{E}\bigl[g(Y)\,\mathbb{E}[f(X)\mid Z,Y]\,\mathbb{E}[k(W)\mid Z,Y]\,\big|\,Z\bigr].
$$
The hypothesis $X\perp Y\mid Z$ gives $\mathbb{E}[f(X)\mid Z,Y]=\mathbb{E}[f(X)\mid Z]$, by the same
argument as in (G3) with the roles of $W$ and $Y$ exchanged. Pulling the now $Z$-measurable factor
$\mathbb{E}[f(X)\mid Z]$ outside,
$$
\mathbb{E}[f(X)g(Y)k(W)\mid Z]
=\mathbb{E}[f(X)\mid Z]\,\mathbb{E}\bigl[g(Y)k(W)\,\big|\,Z\bigr],
$$
where we recognized $\mathbb{E}[g(Y)\,\mathbb{E}[k(W)\mid Z,Y]\mid Z]=\mathbb{E}[g(Y)k(W)\mid Z]$ by the
tower property. Since $f,g,k$ were arbitrary bounded measurable functions, $X\perp(Y,W)\mid Z$.

**(G5)** Under strict positivity of the joint density the proof factors the density logarithmically and
is given in @hernan2020whatif (technical points) and, in full, in Pearl's development of graphical
models; we cite it rather than reproduce the density bookkeeping. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Reading the weak-union step (G3).** In words, (G3) says that if $X$ is irrelevant to the pair $(Y,W)$
once $Z$ is known, then revealing $W$ as well cannot make $X$ relevant to $Y$. The proof first extracts
$X\perp W\mid Z$ (so conditioning on $W$ does not change $X$'s conditional law), substitutes that fact
inside the conditional expectation, and matches both sides against every test function of $W$. Each "by
the defining property" step is just the totals-match rule of @def-conditional-expectation applied to a new
event, and "taking out what is known" pulls out the factors already determined by the conditioning
variables.
:::

This is result A.6. The first four axioms hold with no further assumption; only intersection requires
positivity, which in the indirect-comparison setting is exactly the overlap condition that the target
covariate density be positive wherever the source density is.

::: {.remark}
**Why this matters.** These rules are the symbolic engine behind covariate adjustment. The
propensity-score reduction of Chapter 10, that adjusting for the scalar propensity score suffices whenever
adjusting for the full covariate vector suffices, is a chain of weak union and contraction applied to
$T\perp (Y(0),Y(1))\mid X$. The positivity hypothesis on (G5) is the same overlap condition that
population-adjusted indirect comparison requires: the target covariate density must be positive wherever
the source density is, or the adjustment is not identified.
:::

## Two fundamental inequalities {#sec-inequalities}

We now prove the two inequalities that drive the qualitative phenomena of the rest of the book.

### Jensen's inequality {#sec-jensen}

Recall that $\varphi:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ is **convex** if
$\varphi(\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y)\le\lambda\varphi(x)+(1-\lambda)\varphi(y)$ for all $x,y$ and
$\lambda\in[0,1]$, and **strictly convex** if the inequality is strict whenever $x\ne y$ and
$\lambda\in(0,1)$. The geometric content of convexity is that the graph lies above each of its tangent
or supporting lines; the following lemma makes that precise and is the engine of the proof.

::: {#lem-supporting-line}
## Supporting line for a convex function
Let $\varphi:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ be convex and $t\in\mathbb{R}$. The one-sided derivatives
$\varphi'_{-}(t)$ and $\varphi'_{+}(t)$ exist with $\varphi'_{-}(t)\le\varphi'_{+}(t)$, and for every
slope $a\in[\varphi'_{-}(t),\varphi'_{+}(t)]$,
$$
\varphi(x)\ge\varphi(t)+a\,(x-t)\qquad\text{for all }x\in\mathbb{R},
$$ {#eq-supporting-line}
with strict inequality for every $x\ne t$ when $\varphi$ is strictly convex.
:::

::: {.proof}
The **slope inequality** for convex $\varphi$ states that for $s<t<u$,
$$
\frac{\varphi(t)-\varphi(s)}{t-s}\le\frac{\varphi(u)-\varphi(s)}{u-s}\le\frac{\varphi(u)-\varphi(t)}{u-t}.
$$
To see it, write $t=\lambda s+(1-\lambda)u$ with $\lambda=\frac{u-t}{u-s}\in(0,1)$, so that
$1-\lambda=\frac{t-s}{u-s}$; convexity gives $\varphi(t)\le\lambda\varphi(s)+(1-\lambda)\varphi(u)$.
Subtracting $\varphi(s)$ from both sides,
$$
\varphi(t)-\varphi(s)\le(1-\lambda)\bigl(\varphi(u)-\varphi(s)\bigr)=\frac{t-s}{u-s}\bigl(\varphi(u)-\varphi(s)\bigr),
$$
and dividing by the positive length $t-s$ gives the left inequality. Subtracting $\varphi(u)$ from both
sides instead,
$$
\varphi(t)-\varphi(u)\le\lambda\bigl(\varphi(s)-\varphi(u)\bigr)=\frac{u-t}{u-s}\bigl(\varphi(s)-\varphi(u)\bigr),
$$
and dividing by the positive length $u-t$, then multiplying through by $-1$ to flip the sign, gives the
right inequality. The
inequality shows that the difference quotient $x\mapsto\frac{\varphi(x)-\varphi(t)}{x-t}$ is
nondecreasing on each side of $t$ and that every quotient with $x<t$ is at most every quotient with
$x>t$. Hence the right derivative $\varphi'_{+}(t)=\inf_{x>t}\frac{\varphi(x)-\varphi(t)}{x-t}$ and the
left derivative $\varphi'_{-}(t)=\sup_{x<t}\frac{\varphi(x)-\varphi(t)}{x-t}$ exist and satisfy
$\varphi'_{-}(t)\le\varphi'_{+}(t)$. For $a$ in this interval and $x>t$ we have
$\frac{\varphi(x)-\varphi(t)}{x-t}\ge\varphi'_{+}(t)\ge a$, which rearranges to @eq-supporting-line; for
$x<t$ we have $\frac{\varphi(x)-\varphi(t)}{x-t}\le\varphi'_{-}(t)\le a$, and multiplying by the negative
quantity $x-t$ reverses the inequality to give @eq-supporting-line again. Strict convexity makes every
difference quotient strictly monotone, so the inequalities are strict for $x\ne t$. $\square$
:::

::: {#thm-jensen}
## Jensen's inequality
Let $\varphi:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ be convex and let $X\in L^1$ with $\varphi(X)\in L^1$. Then
$$
\varphi\bigl(\mathbb{E}[X]\bigr)\le\mathbb{E}\bigl[\varphi(X)\bigr].
$$ {#eq-jensen}
If $\varphi$ is strictly convex and $X$ is nondegenerate, that is, not almost surely constant, the
inequality is strict.
:::

::: {.proof}
Set $t=\mathbb{E}[X]$ and choose any slope $a\in[\varphi'_{-}(t),\varphi'_{+}(t)]$. By
@lem-supporting-line, the supporting-line inequality holds pointwise:
$\varphi(X)\ge\varphi(t)+a\,(X-t)$ almost surely. Both sides are integrable, $\varphi(X)$ by hypothesis
and the right side because $X\in L^1$, so taking expectations and using linearity,
$$
\mathbb{E}[\varphi(X)]\ge\varphi(t)+a\,\bigl(\mathbb{E}[X]-t\bigr)=\varphi(t)=\varphi(\mathbb{E}[X]),
$$
because $\mathbb{E}[X]-t=0$. This is @eq-jensen. If $\varphi$ is strictly convex and $X$ is
nondegenerate, then @lem-supporting-line gives $\varphi(X)>\varphi(t)+a(X-t)$ on the event
$\{X\ne t\}$, which has positive probability; the expectation of a random variable that is everywhere at
least a given quantity and strictly greater on a set of positive probability is strictly greater, so the
inequality in @eq-jensen is strict. $\square$
:::

This is result A.7. The **Jensen gap** $\mathbb{E}[\varphi(X)]-\varphi(\mathbb{E}[X])\ge 0$ measures the
failure of $\varphi$ to commute with the expectation. The smallest instructive instance is
$\varphi(x)=x^2$, for which the gap is exactly the variance:
$\mathbb{E}[X^2]-(\mathbb{E}X)^2=\mathrm{Var}(X)$. In later chapters $\varphi$ will be the inverse link
$g^{-1}$ of a generalized linear model, and the gap will be aggregation bias and non-collapsibility, made
concrete in the next example.

::: {#exm-jensen-logit}
## Aggregation bias on the logit scale
This is the instance of Jensen that drives non-collapsibility. Consider a population in two equally sized
severity strata whose response risks are the active-arm risks of @exm-toy-trial, $p_{\text{low}}=0.5$ and
$p_{\text{high}}=0.9$. On the log-odds (logit) scale the two linear predictors are
$$
\eta_{\text{low}}=\mathrm{logit}(0.5)=0,\qquad \eta_{\text{high}}=\mathrm{logit}(0.9)=\ln 9=2\ln 3.
$$
The true population-average risk is the average of the two risks,
$$
\mathbb{E}\bigl[\mathrm{logit}^{-1}(\eta)\bigr]=\tfrac12(0.5)+\tfrac12(0.9)=0.70.
$$
The risk you would predict by first averaging on the linear-predictor scale and then transforming back is
$$
\mathrm{logit}^{-1}\bigl(\mathbb{E}[\eta]\bigr)
=\mathrm{logit}^{-1}\!\Bigl(\tfrac12\cdot 0+\tfrac12\cdot 2\ln 3\Bigr)
=\mathrm{logit}^{-1}(\ln 3)=\frac{3}{1+3}=0.75.
$$
The two disagree, $0.70\ne 0.75$: the inverse link of the average linear predictor overstates the
population risk by five percentage points. Since $\mathrm{logit}^{-1}$ is concave for $\eta\ge 0$,
@thm-jensen predicts the direction, $\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{logit}^{-1}(\eta)]\le\mathrm{logit}^{-1}(\mathbb{E}[\eta])$.
A model fit on the logit scale therefore cannot be collapsed to a population by averaging linear
predictors and back-transforming; this gap is the source of the non-collapsibility of the odds ratio
studied in Chapter 11.
:::

::: {.remark}
**Why this matters.** Jensen's inequality is why "the effect in the average patient" and "the average
effect over patients" are different numbers whenever the link is nonlinear. Aggregation bias in
meta-regression, the non-collapsibility of odds and hazard ratios, and the failure of marginal effects to
transport across populations are all the Jensen gap of @exm-jensen-logit wearing different clothes. The
entire purpose of population adjustment, MAIC, STC, and ML-NMR, is to compute the average on the correct
side of this inequality.
:::

### The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality for expectations {#sec-cauchy-schwarz}

::: {#thm-cauchy-schwarz-exp}
## Cauchy-Schwarz for expectations
For random variables $X,Y\in L^2$,
$$
\bigl(\mathbb{E}[XY]\bigr)^2\le\mathbb{E}[X^2]\,\mathbb{E}[Y^2],
$$ {#eq-cauchy-schwarz}
with equality if and only if $X=0$ almost surely, or $Y=cX$ almost surely for some constant $c$.
:::

::: {.proof}
First note $XY\in L^1$, since $|XY|\le\tfrac12(X^2+Y^2)$ by the inequality of arithmetic and geometric
means, so the left side is defined. If $\mathbb{E}[X^2]=0$ then $X=0$ almost surely, both sides are $0$,
and the equality case holds. Assume $\mathbb{E}[X^2]>0$. For every $\lambda\in\mathbb{R}$, nonnegativity
of a square and linearity give
$$
0\le\mathbb{E}\bigl[(Y-\lambda X)^2\bigr]
=\mathbb{E}[Y^2]-2\lambda\,\mathbb{E}[XY]+\lambda^2\,\mathbb{E}[X^2].
$$
The right side is a quadratic in $\lambda$ with positive leading coefficient that is nonnegative for all
real $\lambda$; hence its discriminant is nonpositive,
$$
4\bigl(\mathbb{E}[XY]\bigr)^2-4\,\mathbb{E}[X^2]\,\mathbb{E}[Y^2]\le 0,
$$
which is @eq-cauchy-schwarz. Equality holds if and only if the discriminant is zero, that is, if and
only if the quadratic has a real double root $\lambda^{*}$, at which
$\mathbb{E}[(Y-\lambda^{*}X)^2]=0$, equivalently $Y=\lambda^{*}X$ almost surely. $\square$
:::

This is result A.8. Applied to a centered pair $(X-\mathbb{E}X,\,Y-\mathbb{E}Y)$ it gives the covariance
bound $\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)^2\le\mathrm{Var}(X)\,\mathrm{Var}(Y)$, so the correlation coefficient lies in
$[-1,1]$. A second instance is the bound behind effective sample size. Take the probability space to be
the index set $\{1,\dots,n\}$ equipped with the **empirical measure** $P(\{i\})=1/n$, and on it the two
random variables $X(i)=w_i$ (the matching weight of patient $i$) and $Y(i)=1$. Then
$\mathbb{E}[XY]=\frac{1}{n}\sum_i w_i$, $\mathbb{E}[X^2]=\frac{1}{n}\sum_i w_i^2$, and
$\mathbb{E}[Y^2]=1$, so @eq-cauchy-schwarz reads
$$
\Bigl(\frac{1}{n}\sum_i w_i\Bigr)^2\le\frac{1}{n}\sum_i w_i^2,
\qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad
\Bigl(\sum_i w_i\Bigr)^2\le n\sum_i w_i^2.
$$
Rearranged, this is the effective sample size bound
$\mathrm{ESS}=\bigl(\sum_i w_i\bigr)^2/\sum_i w_i^2\le n$, with equality if and only if all weights are
equal.

::: {.remark}
**Why this matters.** The ESS bound is the formal reason matching-adjusted indirect comparison loses
precision under poor covariate overlap. When the source and target populations differ sharply the weights
$w_i$ become very unequal, the inequality is far from tight, and the effective sample size collapses well
below $n$. Cauchy-Schwarz here is not an abstract nicety; it quantifies the precision cost of reweighting,
which Chapter 18 develops in full.
:::

We also record the multidimensional integration theorem, result A.10, which licenses every interchange
of the order of integration in the aggregate likelihoods of Part V.

::: {#thm-fubini-tonelli}
## Fubini-Tonelli (cited)
Let $(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{A},\mu)$ and $(\mathcal{Y},\mathcal{B},\nu)$ be $\sigma$-finite measure
spaces ($\sigma$-finite means each space can be covered by countably many pieces of finite measure;
Lebesgue measure and every probability measure qualify). If $f:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}\to[0,\infty]$ is jointly measurable, then the two iterated
integrals and the double integral against the product measure $\mu\otimes\nu$ all agree (Tonelli). If
instead $f$ is real-valued with $\int|f|\,d(\mu\otimes\nu)<\infty$, the iterated integrals are
well-defined almost everywhere and equal the double integral (Fubini).
:::

A proof is in @billingsley1995, §18.

::: {.remark}
**Why this matters.** Fubini-Tonelli is the license to average in stages. In Part V an aggregate
likelihood is built by first averaging an individual outcome over a covariate distribution within a study,
then combining across studies or arms; the theorem guarantees that the order of these nested averages does
not change the answer, so the integral defining the aggregate model is well posed.
:::

We turn to the structural fact that links the covariance matrix to
the positive-definite theory of @sec-cov-psd.

## Covariance matrices are positive semidefinite {#sec-cov-psd}

The covariance matrix is not an arbitrary symmetric matrix; the quadratic-form identity
@eq-var-quadratic-form forces it into the positive semidefinite cone, and conversely every member of
that cone arises as a covariance. This is the precise sense in which the spectral theory of Chapter 3 is
the right language for second moments. Recall from Chapter 3 the characterization
@thm-pd-characterization, that a symmetric matrix $A$ is positive semidefinite ($A\succeq 0$) if and
only if $\mathbf{a}^{\top}A\,\mathbf{a}\ge 0$ for all $\mathbf{a}$, equivalently if and only if all its
eigenvalues are nonnegative, and the spectral theorem @thm-spectral-theorem, that a symmetric $A$
factors as $A=Q\Lambda Q^{\top}$ with $Q$ orthogonal and $\Lambda$ diagonal.

::: {#thm-cov-psd}
## Covariance matrices and the PSD cone
Let $\mathbf{X}$ be a random vector in $\mathbb{R}^p$ with all components in $L^2$ and covariance matrix
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=\mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf{X})$. Then $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ is symmetric and positive
semidefinite. Conversely, every symmetric positive semidefinite $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times p}$
is the covariance matrix of some random vector.
:::

::: {.proof}
Symmetry holds because $\Sigma_{ij}=\mathrm{Cov}(X_i,X_j)=\mathrm{Cov}(X_j,X_i)=\Sigma_{ji}$. For
positive semidefiniteness, fix $\mathbf{a}\in\mathbb{R}^p$. By the quadratic-form identity
@eq-var-quadratic-form,
$$
\mathbf{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\,\mathbf{a}=\mathrm{Var}(\mathbf{a}^{\top}\mathbf{X})\ge 0,
$$
since a variance is the expectation of a square and hence nonnegative. As this holds for every
$\mathbf{a}$, the characterization @thm-pd-characterization gives $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\succeq 0$.

For the converse, let $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\succeq 0$ be symmetric. By the spectral theorem
@thm-spectral-theorem write $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=Q\Lambda Q^{\top}$ with $Q$ orthogonal and
$\Lambda=\mathrm{diag}(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_p)$; by @thm-pd-characterization every $\lambda_i\ge 0$,
so the **symmetric square root**
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2}:=Q\,\mathrm{diag}(\sqrt{\lambda_1},\dots,\sqrt{\lambda_p})\,Q^{\top}$ is a
well-defined symmetric matrix with $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2}=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$.
Let $\mathbf{Z}=(Z_1,\dots,Z_p)^{\top}$ have independent components with $\mathbb{E}[Z_i]=0$ and
$\mathrm{Var}(Z_i)=1$, so that $\mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf{Z})=I_p$, and set
$\mathbf{X}=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2}\mathbf{Z}$. Then $\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{X}]=\mathbf{0}$ and, using
bilinearity of covariance under linear maps,
$$
\mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf{X})=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2}\,\mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf{Z})\,\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2}
=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2}I_p\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2}=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}.\qquad\square
$$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Why this matters.** This theorem lets us treat "a covariance matrix" and "a positive semidefinite
matrix" as the same object. Practically, it guarantees that any valid covariance we estimate can be
factored as $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2}$ and simulated from, and it is the reason
the normal-approximation likelihoods of network meta-analysis, whose inputs are estimated covariance
matrices of log-effects, are coherent probability models rather than formal expressions.
:::

The converse construction $\mathbf{X}=\boldsymbol{\mu}+\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2}\mathbf{Z}$, with
$\mathbf{Z}$ a vector of standard normals, is exactly how we will build the general multivariate normal
in @sec-mvn.

## Moment generating functions {#sec-mgf}

How can we find the distribution of a sum of independent variables without grinding through a convolution
integral, and how can we read off moments without integrating against the density each time? Both are
answered by a single transform. A distribution is often most conveniently encoded not through its density
but through a transform that turns convolution into multiplication and differentiation into moment
extraction.

::: {#def-mgf}
## Moment generating function
The **moment generating function** (MGF) of a random vector $X$ in $\mathbb{R}^p$ is
$$
M_X(\mathbf{t}):=\mathbb{E}\bigl[e^{\mathbf{t}^{\top}X}\bigr],\qquad\mathbf{t}\in\mathbb{R}^p,
$$
defined for those $\mathbf{t}$ at which the expectation is finite. We say the MGF **exists** if it is
finite for all $\mathbf{t}$ in some open neighborhood of the origin. For a scalar $X$ this reads
$M_X(t)=\mathbb{E}[e^{tX}]$.
:::

::: {.remark}
**Reader translation.** The moment generating function is a calculation device, not a modeling
assumption. It repackages a whole distribution as one function of a dummy variable $\mathbf{t}$, with two
payoffs: differentiating it at the origin reads off the moments (@thm-mgf-moments), and multiplying two of
them yields the distribution of a sum (@thm-mgf-sum) without the difficult convolution that densities
would require. We use it precisely to avoid repeated density integrations when establishing facts about
the Poisson, the normal, and the multivariate normal. Following the notation chapter we keep the subscript
unbolded, $M_X$, even when $X$ is a vector.
:::

The name is justified by the next result: where the MGF exists, it determines all moments by
differentiation at the origin.

::: {#thm-mgf-moments}
## Moments from the MGF
Suppose the scalar MGF $M_X$ is finite on $(-\delta,\delta)$ for some $\delta>0$. Then $X$ has finite
moments of every order, $M_X$ is infinitely differentiable on $(-\delta,\delta)$, and
$$
M_X^{(k)}(0)=\mathbb{E}[X^k],\qquad k=0,1,2,\dots.
$$
:::

::: {.proof}
Fix $0<r<\delta$. The elementary bound $|x|^k\le k!\,r^{-k}e^{r|x|}$, valid because $e^{r|x|}\ge
(r|x|)^k/k!$, together with $e^{r|x|}\le e^{rx}+e^{-rx}$, gives
$|X|^k\le k!\,r^{-k}\bigl(e^{rX}+e^{-rX}\bigr)$. The right side is integrable, as
$\mathbb{E}[e^{\pm rX}]=M_X(\pm r)<\infty$, so $\mathbb{E}|X|^k<\infty$ for every $k$. To differentiate
under the expectation, fix $t\in(-\delta,\delta)$ and choose $r'$ with $|t|<r'<\delta$. For real $h$
with $0<|h|<r'-|t|$ the difference quotient $\frac{e^{(t+h)X}-e^{tX}}{h}$ equals $Xe^{\theta X}$ for some
$\theta$ between $t$ and $t+h$, by the mean value theorem, and since $|\theta|<r'$ it is bounded in
absolute value by $|X|e^{r'|X|}$. Choosing $r''$ with $r'<r''<\delta$, the elementary bound
$u\,e^{r'u}\le C\,e^{r''u}$ for $u\ge 0$, valid with $C=\frac{1}{e\,(r''-r')}$ because the function
$u\mapsto u\,e^{-(r''-r')u}$ attains its maximum over $u\ge 0$ at $u=1/(r''-r')$ with value $C$, gives
$|X|e^{r'|X|}\le C\bigl(e^{r''X}+e^{-r''X}\bigr)$, a
dominating variable that is integrable because $M_X(\pm r'')<\infty$. As $h\to 0$ the quotients converge
pointwise to $Xe^{tX}$, so the dominated convergence theorem @thm-dominated-convergence yields
$M_X'(t)=\mathbb{E}[Xe^{tX}]$. Applying the same argument to $x\mapsto x^{j}e^{tx}$, whose increments are
dominated by $|X|^{j+1}e^{r'|X|}\le C_j\bigl(e^{r''X}+e^{-r''X}\bigr)$, gives by induction
$M_X^{(k)}(t)=\mathbb{E}[X^k e^{tX}]$ for every $k$ and every $t\in(-\delta,\delta)$. Evaluating at $t=0$
gives $M_X^{(k)}(0)=\mathbb{E}[X^k]$. $\square$
:::

The MGF also identifies the law and turns independent sums into products. The first property is deep and
is cited; the second we prove.

::: {#thm-mgf-uniqueness}
## Uniqueness and factorization (uniqueness cited)
If two random vectors $X,Y$ have MGFs that are finite and equal on a common neighborhood of the origin,
then $X$ and $Y$ have the same law. Consequently, if the joint MGF of $(X,Y)$ factors as
$M_{(X,Y)}(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{t})=M_X(\mathbf{s})\,M_Y(\mathbf{t})$ on a neighborhood of the origin, then
$X\perp Y$.
:::

::: {.proof}
The uniqueness statement is classical and is proved by analytic continuation of the MGF to the complex
plane, where it becomes the characteristic function whose inversion recovers the law; see
@billingsley1995, §30. For the factorization consequence, let $\widetilde{P}=P_X\otimes P_Y$ be the
product of the marginal laws, the law of an independent pair $(\widetilde{X},\widetilde{Y})$ with the
given marginals. By @thm-fubini-tonelli,
$$
\mathbb{E}_{\widetilde P}\bigl[e^{\mathbf{s}^{\top}\widetilde X+\mathbf{t}^{\top}\widetilde Y}\bigr]
=\mathbb{E}\bigl[e^{\mathbf{s}^{\top}X}\bigr]\,\mathbb{E}\bigl[e^{\mathbf{t}^{\top}Y}\bigr]
=M_X(\mathbf{s})\,M_Y(\mathbf{t}),
$$
which by hypothesis equals the joint MGF of $(X,Y)$ near the origin. By the uniqueness statement applied
to the pair, the joint law of $(X,Y)$ equals the product law $\widetilde{P}$, which is the definition of
$X\perp Y$. $\square$
:::

::: {#thm-mgf-sum}
## MGF of a sum of independent variables
If $X\perp Y$ are scalar random variables whose MGFs are finite on a common neighborhood of the origin,
then $M_{X+Y}(t)=M_X(t)\,M_Y(t)$ there. More generally, for mutually independent $X_1,\dots,X_n$,
$M_{X_1+\cdots+X_n}(t)=\prod_{i=1}^n M_{X_i}(t)$.
:::

::: {.proof}
By independence and the factorization of expectations of products of functions of independent variables,
$$
M_{X+Y}(t)=\mathbb{E}\bigl[e^{t(X+Y)}\bigr]=\mathbb{E}\bigl[e^{tX}e^{tY}\bigr]
=\mathbb{E}[e^{tX}]\,\mathbb{E}[e^{tY}]=M_X(t)M_Y(t),
$$
the middle equality justified by @thm-fubini-tonelli applied to the nonnegative integrand
$e^{tx}e^{ty}$ against the product law. The $n$-fold statement follows by induction, since a partial sum
$X_1+\cdots+X_{n-1}$ is independent of $X_n$. $\square$
:::

We record two further elementary identities used repeatedly. For an affine transform,
$M_{a+bX}(t)=e^{at}M_X(bt)$, immediate from
$\mathbb{E}[e^{t(a+bX)}]=e^{at}\mathbb{E}[e^{(tb)X}]$; and for a vector $X$ and matrix $B$,
$M_{BX}(\mathbf{t})=M_X(B^{\top}\mathbf{t})$. These power the multivariate normal calculus of @sec-mvn.

## Core distributions {#sec-distributions}

We pause the abstract development to collect the concrete distributions we will quote later, computing the
mean, variance, and moment generating function of each once so the arithmetic need not be repeated. We
then return to the multivariate normal in @sec-mvn, which leans on the univariate normal recorded here.
The arithmetic in this section is elementary and worth carrying out once.

::: {#def-bernoulli}
## Bernoulli
$X\sim\mathrm{Ber}(p)$, $p\in[0,1]$, takes the value $1$ with probability $p$ and $0$ with probability
$1-p$. Then $\mathbb{E}[X]=p$, $\mathrm{Var}(X)=p(1-p)$, and $M_X(t)=(1-p)+pe^{t}$.
:::

The mean is $p\cdot 1+(1-p)\cdot 0=p$; the second moment is $\mathbb{E}[X^2]=p$ since $X^2=X$, so the
variance is $p-p^2=p(1-p)$; the MGF is $(1-p)e^{0}+pe^{t}$.

::: {#def-binomial}
## Binomial
$X\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n,p)$ is the number of successes in $n$ independent $\mathrm{Ber}(p)$ trials, with
probability mass function $P(X=k)=\binom{n}{k}p^k(1-p)^{n-k}$ for $k=0,\dots,n$. Then
$\mathbb{E}[X]=np$, $\mathrm{Var}(X)=np(1-p)$, and $M_X(t)=\bigl((1-p)+pe^{t}\bigr)^n$.
:::

Writing $X=\sum_{i=1}^n B_i$ with $B_i\sim\mathrm{Ber}(p)$ independent, linearity gives
$\mathbb{E}[X]=np$, independence gives $\mathrm{Var}(X)=\sum_i\mathrm{Var}(B_i)=np(1-p)$, and
@thm-mgf-sum gives $M_X(t)=\prod_i\bigl((1-p)+pe^t\bigr)=\bigl((1-p)+pe^t\bigr)^n$.

::: {#def-poisson}
## Poisson
$X\sim\mathrm{Poi}(\lambda)$, $\lambda>0$, has $P(X=k)=e^{-\lambda}\lambda^k/k!$ for
$k=0,1,2,\dots$. Then $\mathbb{E}[X]=\lambda$, $\mathrm{Var}(X)=\lambda$, and
$M_X(t)=\exp\bigl(\lambda(e^t-1)\bigr)$.
:::

The MGF is
$M_X(t)=\sum_{k\ge 0}e^{tk}e^{-\lambda}\lambda^k/k!
=e^{-\lambda}\sum_{k\ge 0}(\lambda e^t)^k/k!=e^{-\lambda}e^{\lambda e^t}=\exp(\lambda(e^t-1))$,
the interchange of sum and the implicit expectation being an absolutely convergent series. Then
$M_X'(t)=\lambda e^t M_X(t)$ gives $\mathbb{E}[X]=M_X'(0)=\lambda$, and
$M_X''(0)=\lambda+\lambda^2=\mathbb{E}[X^2]$ gives $\mathrm{Var}(X)=\lambda$, by @thm-mgf-moments. The
Poisson is the law of rare events, made precise through the MGF.

::: {#thm-poisson-limit}
## Poisson limit of the binomial
Fix $\lambda>0$. If $X_n\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n,\lambda/n)$, then $M_{X_n}(t)\to\exp(\lambda(e^t-1))$ for
every $t$, and hence $X_n\xrightarrow{d}\mathrm{Poi}(\lambda)$.
:::

::: {.proof}
By @def-binomial,
$$
M_{X_n}(t)=\Bigl(1-\tfrac{\lambda}{n}+\tfrac{\lambda}{n}e^t\Bigr)^n
=\Bigl(1+\tfrac{\lambda(e^t-1)}{n}\Bigr)^n\longrightarrow\exp\bigl(\lambda(e^t-1)\bigr),
$$
using the standard limit $(1+a/n)^n\to e^a$ with $a=\lambda(e^t-1)$. The limit is the MGF of
$\mathrm{Poi}(\lambda)$ from @def-poisson, finite in a neighborhood of $0$; by the continuity theorem for
moment generating functions, convergence of MGFs on a neighborhood of the origin implies convergence in
distribution (see @billingsley1995, §30). $\square$
:::

The continuity theorem is cited here; a quantitative total-variation version of this Poisson
approximation, due to Le Cam, is proved in the multilevel network meta-regression chapters of Part V.
The next distribution generalizes the binomial by allowing the success probabilities to differ across
trials, and it is the law of an aggregate event count when individual risks vary, which is exactly the
situation in covariate-adjusted meta-analysis.

::: {#def-poisson-binomial}
## Poisson binomial
Let $\mathbf{p}=(p_1,\dots,p_n)\in[0,1]^n$ and let $B_1,\dots,B_n$ be independent with
$B_i\sim\mathrm{Ber}(p_i)$. The law of $X=\sum_{i=1}^n B_i$ is the **Poisson binomial distribution**
$\mathrm{PoBin}(\mathbf{p})$. Its probability mass function is
$$
P(X=k)=\sum_{\substack{A\subseteq\{1,\dots,n\}\\ |A|=k}}\ \prod_{i\in A}p_i\prod_{i\notin A}(1-p_i),
\qquad k=0,\dots,n,
$$
its mean and variance are
$$
\mathbb{E}[X]=\sum_{i=1}^n p_i,\qquad \mathrm{Var}(X)=\sum_{i=1}^n p_i(1-p_i),
$$
and its MGF is $M_X(t)=\prod_{i=1}^n\bigl((1-p_i)+p_i e^t\bigr)$.
:::

::: {.remark}
**Reader translation.** The Poisson binomial is the law of a head count when each coin has its own bias.
If $100$ patients each carry their own baseline risk $p_i$ of an event, the total number of events is
$\mathrm{PoBin}(\mathbf{p})$, not $\mathrm{Bin}(100,\bar p)$; the binomial is only the special case of
equal risks. This is exactly the situation in covariate-adjusted meta-analysis, where individual risks
vary with covariates, and it is why aggregate event counts there are modeled as Poisson binomial.
:::

The mass function lists the disjoint ways to obtain exactly $k$ successes; the mean and variance follow
from linearity and independence as in the binomial case; the MGF follows from @thm-mgf-sum applied to
the Bernoulli MGFs of @def-bernoulli. When all $p_i$ are equal to a common $p$, every quantity reduces
to its $\mathrm{Bin}(n,p)$ counterpart. For a fixed mean $\sum_i p_i$, the variance $\sum_i p_i(1-p_i)
=\sum_i p_i-\sum_i p_i^2$ is largest when the $p_i$ are equal, by convexity of $p\mapsto p^2$; spreading
the risks apart reduces dispersion in the count. We verify all of this numerically in
@sec-prob-worked.

::: {#def-normal}
## Normal
$X\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)$, $\mu\in\mathbb{R}$, $\sigma^2>0$, has density
$$
f_X(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\,\sigma}\exp\!\Bigl(-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\Bigr),\qquad x\in\mathbb{R}.
$$
Then $\mathbb{E}[X]=\mu$, $\mathrm{Var}(X)=\sigma^2$, and $M_X(t)=\exp\bigl(\mu t+\tfrac12\sigma^2t^2\bigr)$.
The case $\mu=0,\sigma^2=1$ is the **standard normal**, with density $\phi$ and CDF $\Phi$.
:::

::: {.remark}
**Reader translation.** The normal is the familiar bell curve; its two parameters are the mean $\mu$ and
the *variance* $\sigma^2$, not the standard deviation. Beware a convention shift coming in @sec-mvn: the
univariate $\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)$ takes a variance as its second argument, while the multivariate
$\mathcal{N}_p(\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\Sigma})$ takes a covariance *matrix*, and the subscript $p$
flags the dimension.
:::

::: {.proof}
That $f_X$ integrates to $1$ is the Gaussian integral
$\int_{\mathbb{R}}e^{-u^2/2}\,du=\sqrt{2\pi}$, established by the polar-coordinates evaluation of its
square. For the MGF, substitute and complete the square in the exponent:
$$
tx-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}
=-\frac{\bigl(x-(\mu+\sigma^2 t)\bigr)^2}{2\sigma^2}+\mu t+\frac{\sigma^2 t^2}{2},
$$
an algebraic identity verified by expanding both sides. Therefore
$$
M_X(t)=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\frac{e^{tx}}{\sqrt{2\pi}\,\sigma}e^{-(x-\mu)^2/2\sigma^2}\,dx
=e^{\mu t+\sigma^2 t^2/2}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\,\sigma}
e^{-(x-(\mu+\sigma^2 t))^2/2\sigma^2}\,dx
=e^{\mu t+\sigma^2 t^2/2},
$$
the remaining integral being that of a $\mathcal{N}(\mu+\sigma^2 t,\sigma^2)$ density, which equals $1$.
Differentiating, $M_X'(t)=(\mu+\sigma^2 t)M_X(t)$ gives $\mathbb{E}[X]=M_X'(0)=\mu$, and
$M_X''(0)=\sigma^2+\mu^2=\mathbb{E}[X^2]$ gives $\mathrm{Var}(X)=\sigma^2$, by @thm-mgf-moments.
$\square$
:::

## The multivariate normal {#sec-mvn}

The multivariate normal is the joint distribution that the central limit theorem produces for sums and
that linear models assume for errors; its closure under affine maps and conditioning is what makes
normal-theory inference tractable. We define it through its MGF, which is the cleanest route and which
handles singular covariance matrices without special cases.

::: {#def-mvn}
## Multivariate normal
A random vector $\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^p$ has the **multivariate normal distribution**
$\mathcal{N}_p(\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\Sigma})$, with mean vector $\boldsymbol{\mu}\in\mathbb{R}^p$
and symmetric positive semidefinite covariance matrix $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times p}$, if
its moment generating function is
$$
M_{\mathbf{X}}(\mathbf{t})=\exp\!\Bigl(\mathbf{t}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\mu}
+\tfrac12\,\mathbf{t}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\,\mathbf{t}\Bigr),\qquad\mathbf{t}\in\mathbb{R}^p.
$$ {#eq-mvn-mgf}
:::

::: {.remark}
**Reader translation.** We define the multivariate normal by its moment generating function rather than a
density for one practical reason: the formula @eq-mvn-mgf makes sense even when $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ is
singular, whereas the density @eq-mvn-density needs $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}$ and breaks down. Singular
covariance is not exotic; it is exactly what arises when one component is a deterministic linear
combination of the others, the probabilistic face of perfect collinearity in a design matrix. The MGF
definition handles the collinear and the full-rank cases with a single formula.
:::

The definition is consistent: such a law exists and is unique. Uniqueness is @thm-mgf-uniqueness.
Existence is the construction $\mathbf{X}=\boldsymbol{\mu}+\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2}\mathbf{Z}$ with
$\mathbf{Z}=(Z_1,\dots,Z_p)^{\top}$ a vector of independent standard normals, exactly the construction of
@thm-cov-psd. Indeed its MGF is, by independence and the standard-normal MGF $\mathbb{E}[e^{sZ_i}]=e^{s^2/2}$,
$$
\mathbb{E}\bigl[e^{\mathbf{t}^{\top}(\boldsymbol{\mu}+\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2}\mathbf{Z})}\bigr]
=e^{\mathbf{t}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\mu}}\prod_{i=1}^p\mathbb{E}\bigl[e^{(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2}\mathbf{t})_i Z_i}\bigr]
=e^{\mathbf{t}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\mu}}\exp\!\Bigl(\tfrac12\|\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2}\mathbf{t}\|_2^2\Bigr)
=\exp\!\Bigl(\mathbf{t}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\mu}+\tfrac12\mathbf{t}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{t}\Bigr),
$$
since $\|\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2}\mathbf{t}\|_2^2
=\mathbf{t}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2}\mathbf{t}
=\mathbf{t}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{t}$. Thus @eq-mvn-mgf is the MGF of an honest random vector,
whose mean is $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ and whose covariance is $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ by @thm-cov-psd.

When $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\succ 0$ is nonsingular the law has a density, obtained by the change of
variables from $\mathbf{Z}$.

::: {#prp-mvn-density}
## Density of a nonsingular multivariate normal
If $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\succ 0$, then $\mathcal{N}_p(\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\Sigma})$ has density
$$
f_{\mathbf{X}}(\mathbf{x})=(2\pi)^{-p/2}\,\det(\boldsymbol{\Sigma})^{-1/2}
\exp\!\Bigl(-\tfrac12(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})\Bigr),
\qquad\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^p.
$$ {#eq-mvn-density}
:::

::: {.proof}
The standard normal vector $\mathbf{Z}$ has density
$(2\pi)^{-p/2}\exp(-\tfrac12\mathbf{z}^{\top}\mathbf{z})$, being a product of $p$ standard normal
densities. Since $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\succ 0$, the symmetric square root $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2}$ is
invertible, so $\mathbf{X}=\boldsymbol{\mu}+\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2}\mathbf{Z}$ is an invertible affine
map with inverse $\mathbf{z}=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1/2}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})$ and Jacobian
determinant $\det(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1/2})=\det(\boldsymbol{\Sigma})^{-1/2}$. The change-of-variables
formula for densities gives
$$
f_{\mathbf{X}}(\mathbf{x})=(2\pi)^{-p/2}\exp\!\Bigl(-\tfrac12\|\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1/2}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})\|_2^2\Bigr)\,\det(\boldsymbol{\Sigma})^{-1/2},
$$
and $\|\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1/2}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})\|_2^2
=(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})$, which is
@eq-mvn-density. $\square$
:::

The defining MGF makes the behavior under affine maps a one-line computation, and that single fact
yields marginals, sums, and the normality of every linear combination.

::: {#thm-mvn-linear}
## Affine maps of a multivariate normal
Let $\mathbf{X}\sim\mathcal{N}_p(\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\Sigma})$, let $B\in\mathbb{R}^{q\times p}$,
and let $\mathbf{b}\in\mathbb{R}^q$. Then
$$
\mathbf{Y}=\mathbf{b}+B\mathbf{X}\sim\mathcal{N}_q\bigl(\mathbf{b}+B\boldsymbol{\mu},\,B\boldsymbol{\Sigma}B^{\top}\bigr).
$$
In particular every subvector of $\mathbf{X}$ is multivariate normal, and for any
$\mathbf{a}\in\mathbb{R}^p$ the scalar $\mathbf{a}^{\top}\mathbf{X}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\mu},\mathbf{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{a})$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Compute the MGF of $\mathbf{Y}$ for $\mathbf{t}\in\mathbb{R}^q$, using the affine and matrix identities
recorded after @thm-mgf-sum and the defining MGF @eq-mvn-mgf of $\mathbf{X}$:
$$
