M_{\mathbf{Y}}(\mathbf{t})=\mathbb{E}\bigl[e^{\mathbf{t}^{\top}(\mathbf{b}+B\mathbf{X})}\bigr]
=e^{\mathbf{t}^{\top}\mathbf{b}}\,M_{\mathbf{X}}(B^{\top}\mathbf{t})
=e^{\mathbf{t}^{\top}\mathbf{b}}\exp\!\Bigl((B^{\top}\mathbf{t})^{\top}\boldsymbol{\mu}
+\tfrac12(B^{\top}\mathbf{t})^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}(B^{\top}\mathbf{t})\Bigr).
$$
The exponent equals
$\mathbf{t}^{\top}(\mathbf{b}+B\boldsymbol{\mu})+\tfrac12\mathbf{t}^{\top}(B\boldsymbol{\Sigma}B^{\top})\mathbf{t}$,
so $M_{\mathbf{Y}}$ is the MGF @eq-mvn-mgf with mean $\mathbf{b}+B\boldsymbol{\mu}$ and covariance
$B\boldsymbol{\Sigma}B^{\top}$, the latter symmetric positive semidefinite because
$\mathbf{s}^{\top}B\boldsymbol{\Sigma}B^{\top}\mathbf{s}=(B^{\top}\mathbf{s})^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}(B^{\top}\mathbf{s})\ge 0$.
By @thm-mgf-uniqueness, $\mathbf{Y}\sim\mathcal{N}_q(\mathbf{b}+B\boldsymbol{\mu},B\boldsymbol{\Sigma}B^{\top})$.
The marginal claim is the case $B=[\,I_k\ \ 0\,]$, $\mathbf{b}=\mathbf{0}$, and the scalar claim is the
case $B=\mathbf{a}^{\top}$. $\square$
:::

::: {#exm-mvn-mini}
## A two-dimensional normal, previewed
To break the abstraction before the conditional-distribution proof, take the bivariate normal we will
carry through @sec-prob-worked,
$$
\boldsymbol{\mu}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix},\qquad
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}.
$$
By @thm-mvn-linear the first coordinate is $X_1\sim\mathcal{N}(1,2)$, read straight off the diagonal, and
the sum $X_1+X_2$ is the affine image with $B=(1,\ 1)$, giving $X_1+X_2\sim\mathcal{N}(3,5)$ since
$B\boldsymbol{\mu}=3$ and $B\boldsymbol{\Sigma}B^{\top}=5$. No densities or integrals are needed; one
matrix multiplication delivers the law of any linear summary. The conditioning, density, and Jensen-gap
calculations for this same matrix are completed in @sec-prob-worked.
:::

For the conditional distribution we need the special feature of normality that uncorrelated jointly
normal blocks are actually independent, a phenomenon that fails for general distributions.

::: {#lem-normal-uncorrelated-independent}
## Uncorrelated jointly normal blocks are independent
Partition $\mathbf{X}\sim\mathcal{N}_p(\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\Sigma})$ as
$\mathbf{X}=(\mathbf{X}_1,\mathbf{X}_2)$ with covariance blocks
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=\begin{pmatrix}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{11}&\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12}\\
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{21}&\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}\end{pmatrix}$. If
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12}=0$, then $\mathbf{X}_1\perp\mathbf{X}_2$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Write $\mathbf{t}=(\mathbf{t}_1,\mathbf{t}_2)$ conformably. When $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12}=0$ (hence
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{21}=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12}^{\top}=0$), the quadratic form in @eq-mvn-mgf splits,
$\mathbf{t}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{t}
=\mathbf{t}_1^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{11}\mathbf{t}_1+\mathbf{t}_2^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}\mathbf{t}_2$,
and the linear form splits as
$\mathbf{t}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\mu}=\mathbf{t}_1^{\top}\boldsymbol{\mu}_1+\mathbf{t}_2^{\top}\boldsymbol{\mu}_2$.
Hence the joint MGF factors,
$$
M_{\mathbf{X}}(\mathbf{t}_1,\mathbf{t}_2)
=\exp\!\Bigl(\mathbf{t}_1^{\top}\boldsymbol{\mu}_1+\tfrac12\mathbf{t}_1^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{11}\mathbf{t}_1\Bigr)
\exp\!\Bigl(\mathbf{t}_2^{\top}\boldsymbol{\mu}_2+\tfrac12\mathbf{t}_2^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}\mathbf{t}_2\Bigr)
=M_{\mathbf{X}_1}(\mathbf{t}_1)\,M_{\mathbf{X}_2}(\mathbf{t}_2),
$$
where the marginal MGFs are read off from @thm-mvn-linear. By the factorization criterion of
@thm-mgf-uniqueness, $\mathbf{X}_1\perp\mathbf{X}_2$. $\square$
:::

::: {#thm-mvn-conditional}
## Conditional distribution of a multivariate normal
Partition $\mathbf{X}\sim\mathcal{N}_p(\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\Sigma})$ as above with
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}\succ 0$. Then the conditional distribution of $\mathbf{X}_1$ given
$\mathbf{X}_2=\mathbf{x}_2$ is multivariate normal,
$$
\mathbf{X}_1\mid\mathbf{X}_2=\mathbf{x}_2\ \sim\
\mathcal{N}\Bigl(\boldsymbol{\mu}_1+\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}^{-1}(\mathbf{x}_2-\boldsymbol{\mu}_2),
\ \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{11}-\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{21}\Bigr).
$$ {#eq-mvn-conditional}
The conditional covariance $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{1\mid 2}:=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{11}-\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{21}$
is the **Schur complement** of $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}$ (the residual covariance left in
$\mathbf{X}_1$ after subtracting the part linearly explained by $\mathbf{X}_2$) and does not depend on
$\mathbf{x}_2$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Define the **regression residual**
$\mathbf{U}:=\mathbf{X}_1-\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}^{-1}\mathbf{X}_2$. The pair
$(\mathbf{U},\mathbf{X}_2)$ is the affine image of $\mathbf{X}$ under
$$
\begin{pmatrix}\mathbf{U}\\\mathbf{X}_2\end{pmatrix}
=\underbrace{\begin{pmatrix}I&-\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}^{-1}\\0&I\end{pmatrix}}_{=:A}
\begin{pmatrix}\mathbf{X}_1\\\mathbf{X}_2\end{pmatrix},
$$
so by @thm-mvn-linear it is jointly multivariate normal. Its cross-covariance vanishes:
$$
\mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf{U},\mathbf{X}_2)
=\mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf{X}_1,\mathbf{X}_2)-\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}^{-1}\mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf{X}_2,\mathbf{X}_2)
=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12}-\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}=0,
$$
so $\mathbf{U}\perp\mathbf{X}_2$ by @lem-normal-uncorrelated-independent. The mean and covariance of
$\mathbf{U}$ are
$$
\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{U}]=\boldsymbol{\mu}_1-\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}_2,
\qquad
\mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf{U})=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{11}-2\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{21}
+\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{21}
=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{1\mid 2},
$$
the cross terms combining because $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{21}=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12}^{\top}$. Now recover
$\mathbf{X}_1=\mathbf{U}+\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}^{-1}\mathbf{X}_2$ and compute the
conditional MGF given $\mathbf{X}_2=\mathbf{x}_2$. Since the factor
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}^{-1}\mathbf{X}_2$ becomes the constant
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}^{-1}\mathbf{x}_2$ under the conditioning, and since
$\mathbf{U}\perp\mathbf{X}_2$ implies $\mathbb{E}[e^{\mathbf{t}^{\top}\mathbf{U}}\mid\mathbf{X}_2]=\mathbb{E}[e^{\mathbf{t}^{\top}\mathbf{U}}]$
(this is the one step that genuinely uses normality: for a general distribution $\mathbf{U}$ could be
uncorrelated with $\mathbf{X}_2$ yet still dependent, but @lem-normal-uncorrelated-independent upgrades
the vanishing cross-covariance to full independence, so conditioning on $\mathbf{X}_2$ leaves the law of
$\mathbf{U}$ untouched),
$$
\mathbb{E}\bigl[e^{\mathbf{t}^{\top}\mathbf{X}_1}\,\big|\,\mathbf{X}_2=\mathbf{x}_2\bigr]
=e^{\mathbf{t}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}^{-1}\mathbf{x}_2}\,
\mathbb{E}\bigl[e^{\mathbf{t}^{\top}\mathbf{U}}\bigr]
=\exp\!\Bigl(\mathbf{t}^{\top}\bigl(\boldsymbol{\mu}_1+\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}^{-1}(\mathbf{x}_2-\boldsymbol{\mu}_2)\bigr)
+\tfrac12\mathbf{t}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{1\mid 2}\mathbf{t}\Bigr),
$$
where the last step substitutes the MGF @eq-mvn-mgf of $\mathbf{U}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{U}],\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{1\mid 2})$ and
collects the linear terms. This is the MGF of the normal law on the right of @eq-mvn-conditional, so by
@thm-mgf-uniqueness the conditional law is as claimed. $\square$
:::

The conditional mean
$\boldsymbol{\mu}_1+\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}^{-1}(\mathbf{x}_2-\boldsymbol{\mu}_2)$
is an affine function of the conditioning value, the population analogue of a linear regression of
$\mathbf{X}_1$ on $\mathbf{X}_2$, and the conditional covariance is constant in $\mathbf{x}_2$. These two
features, linear conditional mean and homoskedastic conditional covariance, are the exact distributional
content of the linear model of Chapter 6 and recur in every normal-approximation likelihood used in the
network meta-analysis chapters.

::: {.remark}
**Why this matters.** The conditional mean of a multivariate normal is linear in the conditioning value,
the population blueprint of linear regression: the regression coefficients are the population object
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}^{-1}$. For indirect comparison this is the object we
integrate over a target population's covariate distribution to produce a population-average prediction,
the move at the heart of ML-NMR in Part V. The constant (homoskedastic) conditional covariance is why the
normal-theory likelihoods of network meta-analysis can carry a single residual variance.
:::

## A fully worked example {#sec-prob-worked}

Where the toy trial of @exm-toy-trial gave us a discrete thread, we now run a continuous one. We carry a
single bivariate normal through every theorem of @sec-cov-psd and @sec-mvn, with arithmetic the reader can
reproduce by hand, and then verify the Poisson binomial mass function of @def-poisson-binomial on a small
example.

### A bivariate normal {#sec-worked-bvn}

Let $\mathbf{X}=(X_1,X_2)^{\top}\sim\mathcal{N}_2(\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\Sigma})$ with
$$
\boldsymbol{\mu}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix},\qquad
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}.
$$

**Positive definiteness (@thm-cov-psd).** The matrix is symmetric. Its eigenvalues solve
$\det(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}-\lambda I)=(2-\lambda)(1-\lambda)-1=\lambda^2-3\lambda+1=0$, giving
$\lambda=\tfrac{3\pm\sqrt5}{2}\approx 2.618$ and $0.382$, both positive, so $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\succ 0$;
its determinant is $\det\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=2\cdot 1-1\cdot 1=1$. We may also confirm positive
semidefiniteness through @eq-var-quadratic-form on a specific direction: for $\mathbf{a}=(1,-1)^{\top}$,
$$
\mathbf{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{a}
=\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix}=1
=\mathrm{Var}(X_1-X_2)=\mathrm{Var}(X_1)+\mathrm{Var}(X_2)-2\,\mathrm{Cov}(X_1,X_2)=2+1-2=1\ge 0,
$$
where $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{a}=(2-1,\,1-1)^{\top}=(1,0)^{\top}$.

**Marginals and correlation (@thm-mvn-linear, @thm-cauchy-schwarz-exp).** Reading off the diagonal,
$X_1\sim\mathcal{N}(1,2)$ and $X_2\sim\mathcal{N}(2,1)$. The correlation is
$\rho=\mathrm{Cov}(X_1,X_2)/\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}(X_1)\mathrm{Var}(X_2)}=1/\sqrt{2\cdot 1}=1/\sqrt2\approx 0.707$,
and Cauchy-Schwarz is the statement $\mathrm{Cov}(X_1,X_2)^2=1\le 2=\mathrm{Var}(X_1)\,\mathrm{Var}(X_2)$,
that is $\rho^2=\tfrac12\le 1$.

**An affine map (@thm-mvn-linear).** Let $Y=X_1+X_2=B\mathbf{X}$ with $B=(1,\ 1)$. Then
$Y\sim\mathcal{N}(B\boldsymbol{\mu},B\boldsymbol{\Sigma}B^{\top})$ with mean
$B\boldsymbol{\mu}=1+2=3$ and variance
$B\boldsymbol{\Sigma}B^{\top}=(1,1)\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}(1,1)^{\top}=(3,2)(1,1)^{\top}=5$,
so $Y\sim\mathcal{N}(3,5)$. The direct check is
$\mathrm{Var}(X_1+X_2)=2+1+2\cdot 1=5$.

**The conditional distribution (@thm-mvn-conditional).** With
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{11}=2$, $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12}=1$, $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}=1$, the
conditional law of $X_1$ given $X_2=x_2$ has mean
$\mu_1+\Sigma_{12}\Sigma_{22}^{-1}(x_2-\mu_2)=1+1\cdot(x_2-2)=x_2-1$ and variance
$\Sigma_{11}-\Sigma_{12}\Sigma_{22}^{-1}\Sigma_{21}=2-1\cdot 1\cdot 1=1$. Hence
$$
X_1\mid X_2=x_2\ \sim\ \mathcal{N}(x_2-1,\ 1),\qquad\text{and at }x_2=4,\quad X_1\mid X_2=4\sim\mathcal{N}(3,1).
$$
Note that the conditional variance $1$ is smaller than the marginal variance $2$: conditioning on the
correlated $X_2$ removes part of the uncertainty in $X_1$. This is the law of total variance
@cor-total-variance in action,
$$
\mathrm{Var}(X_1)=\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{Var}(X_1\mid X_2)]+\mathrm{Var}(\mathbb{E}[X_1\mid X_2])
=1+\mathrm{Var}(X_2-1)=1+1=2,\ \checkmark
$$
because $\mathrm{Var}(X_1\mid X_2)\equiv 1$ is constant and $\mathbb{E}[X_1\mid X_2]=X_2-1$ has variance
$\mathrm{Var}(X_2)=1$.

**The density (@prp-mvn-density).** Since $\det\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=1$ and
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\-1&2\end{pmatrix}$ (one checks
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}=I$), the density is
$$
f_{\mathbf{X}}(\mathbf{x})=\frac{1}{2\pi}\exp\!\Bigl(-\tfrac12\bigl[(x_1-1)^2-2(x_1-1)(x_2-2)+2(x_2-2)^2\bigr]\Bigr),
$$
and at the mean $\mathbf{x}=\boldsymbol{\mu}=(1,2)^{\top}$ this is $f_{\mathbf{X}}(\boldsymbol{\mu})=1/(2\pi)\approx 0.159$.

**The Jensen gap (@thm-jensen).** Apply the convex $\varphi(u)=u^2$ to $X_1\sim\mathcal{N}(1,2)$. The
left side of @eq-jensen is $\varphi(\mathbb{E}[X_1])=1^2=1$; the right side is
$\mathbb{E}[\varphi(X_1)]=\mathbb{E}[X_1^2]=\mathrm{Var}(X_1)+(\mathbb{E}X_1)^2=2+1=3$. The Jensen gap is
$3-1=2$, which is exactly $\mathrm{Var}(X_1)$, as anticipated after @thm-jensen.

### A Poisson binomial count {#sec-worked-pobin}

Take $n=3$ trials with heterogeneous success probabilities
$\mathbf{p}=(0.2,\,0.5,\,0.8)$, so $X\sim\mathrm{PoBin}(\mathbf{p})$ with failure probabilities
$(0.8,\,0.5,\,0.2)$. The mass function of @def-poisson-binomial enumerates subsets:
$$
\begin{aligned}
P(X=0)&=0.8\cdot 0.5\cdot 0.2=0.08,\\
P(X=1)&=0.2\cdot 0.5\cdot 0.2+0.8\cdot 0.5\cdot 0.2+0.8\cdot 0.5\cdot 0.8=0.02+0.08+0.32=0.42,\\
P(X=2)&=0.2\cdot 0.5\cdot 0.2+0.2\cdot 0.5\cdot 0.8+0.8\cdot 0.5\cdot 0.8=0.02+0.08+0.32=0.42,\\
P(X=3)&=0.2\cdot 0.5\cdot 0.8=0.08,
\end{aligned}
$$
which sum to $1$. The mean is $\mathbb{E}[X]=0.2+0.5+0.8=1.5$, confirmed from the mass function as
$0(0.08)+1(0.42)+2(0.42)+3(0.08)=1.5$. The variance is
$\mathrm{Var}(X)=0.2(0.8)+0.5(0.5)+0.8(0.2)=0.16+0.25+0.16=0.57$, confirmed as
$\mathbb{E}[X^2]-(\mathbb{E}X)^2=(0.42+4\cdot 0.42+9\cdot 0.08)-1.5^2=2.82-2.25=0.57$. For contrast, a
binomial $\mathrm{Bin}(3,0.5)$ has the same mean $1.5$ but the larger variance $3(0.5)(0.5)=0.75$;
spreading the per-trial risks apart, at fixed total risk, has reduced the dispersion of the count, in
keeping with the convexity remark after @def-poisson-binomial.

## Notes and references {#sec-prob-notes}

The measure-theoretic framework of @def-probability-space is Kolmogorov's; the closure properties
(@lem-sigma-algebra-closure), the pushforward law (@prp-law-is-measure), the convergence theorems
(@thm-monotone-convergence, @thm-dominated-convergence), conditional expectation through the
Radon-Nikodym theorem (@def-conditional-expectation), Fubini-Tonelli (@thm-fubini-tonelli), and the
uniqueness and continuity theorems for moment generating functions (@thm-mgf-uniqueness,
@thm-poisson-limit) are standard and are proved in @billingsley1995 and @williams1991, which we cite for
the results stated without proof. The load-bearing results of the chapter, the tower property
(@thm-tower-property), Jensen's inequality (@thm-jensen) with its supporting-line lemma
(@lem-supporting-line), the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality for expectations (@thm-cauchy-schwarz-exp), the
positive semidefiniteness of covariance matrices (@thm-cov-psd), and the multivariate normal calculus
(@thm-mvn-linear, @lem-normal-uncorrelated-independent, @thm-mvn-conditional), are proved here in full,
the last group resting on the spectral theorem @thm-spectral-theorem and the positive-definiteness
characterization @thm-pd-characterization of Chapter 3. The multivariate normal theory follows the
treatment in @bingham2010regression, which we recommend for the linear-models reader; the causal framing
of conditional independence and the role of expectation in identification is from @hernan2020whatif.

The development corresponds to results A.1 through A.10 of the proof catalogue: A.1
(@def-probability-space, @lem-sigma-algebra-closure), A.2 (@def-random-variable, @prp-law-is-measure),
A.3 (@thm-monotone-convergence, @thm-dominated-convergence), A.4 (@thm-expectation-linearity,
@thm-tower-property), A.5 (@def-conditional-expectation), A.6 (@def-conditional-independence,
@thm-graphoid-axioms), A.7 (@thm-jensen), A.8 (@thm-cauchy-schwarz-exp), A.9 (@cor-total-expectation),
and A.10 (@thm-fubini-tonelli). The asymptotic tools A.11 through A.13, the delta method, Slutsky's
theorem, and the continuous mapping theorem, belong to the inference chapter that follows. The graphoid
axioms @thm-graphoid-axioms have a machine-checked counterpart in the companion Coq development: the
lemmas `cond_indep_symmetry` and `cond_indep_decomposition` and the theorems `cond_indep_weak_union` and
`cond_indep_contraction` of `theories/ConditionalIndep.v` verify (G1) through (G4) for a discrete joint
model. The foundational facts of @sec-prob-space through @sec-conditional are accepted in that
development as axioms imported from the `mathcomp-analysis` library rather than reproved, as documented
in its `AXIOMS.md`; the mathematical content here is the classical pen-and-paper version.

## Exercises {#sec-prob-exercises}

A starred exercise, marked $\star$, has a full worked solution in Appendix F. The first four exercises are
warm-ups and interpretation; the proof-heavy and starred ones follow.

::: {#exr-reweight-strata}
## Warm-up: reweight two strata
In @exm-toy-trial the control-arm risks are $0.20$ for low-risk patients and $0.50$ for high-risk
patients. The source trial has severity shares $(0.6,0.4)$, while a target population has shares
$(0.3,0.7)$. Using @cor-total-expectation, compute the marginal control response rate in the source and
in the target, and explain in one sentence why they differ even though the within-stratum risks are
identical.
:::

::: {#exr-jensen-logit-interpret}
## Interpretation: average risk versus risk of the average
Two equally sized subgroups have event risks $0.2$ and $0.8$. Compute the population-average risk, and
separately compute the inverse-logit of the average log-odds. Which is larger, and which one should a
decision maker report as the population risk? Relate your answer to @exm-jensen-logit and @thm-jensen.
:::

::: {#exr-ignorability-meaning}
## Interpretation: which independence is ignorability?
Let $T$ be treatment, $X$ baseline covariates, and $Y(0),Y(1)$ the potential outcomes. Using the notation
of @def-conditional-independence, write the conditional-independence statement expressing "a
covariate-adjusted trial assigns treatment without regard to prognosis once covariates are fixed."
Explain in words why $T\perp (Y(0),Y(1))$ without conditioning is a stronger statement, and which one a
covariate-adjusted analysis actually needs.
:::

::: {#exr-pobin-count}
## Computation: a heterogeneous event count
Three patients have event risks $\mathbf{p}=(0.1,0.4,0.6)$. Using @def-poisson-binomial, write out the
full mass function of the event count $X\sim\mathrm{PoBin}(\mathbf{p})$, and verify from it that
$\mathbb{E}[X]=\sum_i p_i$ and $\mathrm{Var}(X)=\sum_i p_i(1-p_i)$. Compare the variance with that of
$\mathrm{Bin}(3,\bar p)$ at the same mean $\bar p=\tfrac13\sum_i p_i$.
:::

::: {#exr-borel-cantelli}
## Closure and a tail event
Using @lem-sigma-algebra-closure, show that for events $\{A_n\}$ the event "$A_n$ occurs for infinitely
many $n$" equals $\limsup_n A_n$ and lies in $\mathcal{F}$. Show further that if
$\sum_n P(A_n)<\infty$ then $P(\limsup_n A_n)=0$. (This is the first Borel-Cantelli lemma; use
$P(\limsup_n A_n)\le P(\bigcup_{n\ge m}A_n)\le\sum_{n\ge m}P(A_n)$ and let $m\to\infty$.)
:::

::: {#exr-variance-identities}
## Variance algebra
For $X,Y\in L^2$ and constants $a,b,c$, prove from @def-variance-covariance that
$\mathrm{Var}(aX+bY+c)=a^2\mathrm{Var}(X)+b^2\mathrm{Var}(Y)+2ab\,\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)$, and deduce that the
correlation coefficient lies in $[-1,1]$ using @thm-cauchy-schwarz-exp.
:::

::: {#exr-jensen-am-gm}
## Jensen at work
Let $X$ be a positive random variable in $L^1$ with $\log X\in L^1$. Using @thm-jensen with a suitable
convex or concave $\varphi$, prove the inequality $\exp(\mathbb{E}[\log X])\le\mathbb{E}[X]$, the
probabilistic form of the arithmetic-geometric mean inequality. Identify the convex function you used
and state when equality holds.
:::

::: {#exr-uncorrelated-not-independent}
## Uncorrelated but dependent
Let $Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ and set $X=Z$, $Y=Z^2$. Show that $\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)=0$ yet $X$ and $Y$ are
not independent. Explain why this does not contradict @lem-normal-uncorrelated-independent. (Hint:
$(X,Y)$ is not jointly normal.)
:::

::: {#exr-mgf-poisson-sum}
## Sums of Poissons
Using @thm-mgf-sum and @def-poisson, prove that if $X\sim\mathrm{Poi}(\lambda)$ and
$Y\sim\mathrm{Poi}(\nu)$ are independent then $X+Y\sim\mathrm{Poi}(\lambda+\nu)$. Then, using
@thm-mvn-linear, prove the normal analogue: independent
$X\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_1,\sigma_1^2)$ and $Y\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_2,\sigma_2^2)$ have
$X+Y\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_1+\mu_2,\sigma_1^2+\sigma_2^2)$.
:::

::: {#exr-conditional-bivariate}
## Bivariate conditioning by hand
For the bivariate normal of @sec-worked-bvn, derive the conditional distribution of $X_2$ given
$X_1=x_1$ using @thm-mvn-conditional, and verify directly that
$\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[X_2\mid X_1]]=\mathbb{E}[X_2]=2$ via @cor-total-expectation. Compute the
conditional variance and confirm the law of total variance @cor-total-variance for $X_2$.
:::

::: {#exr-cov-psd-construction}
## Realizing a covariance (starred)
$\star$ Let $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=\begin{pmatrix}1&\rho\\\rho&1\end{pmatrix}$ with
$\rho\in(-1,1)$. Using @thm-cov-psd, exhibit an explicit random vector with this covariance as a linear
image of a standard normal pair, computing $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2}$ from the spectral decomposition
@thm-spectral-theorem. Determine for which $\rho$ the matrix fails to be positive definite and interpret
the degenerate case via @lem-normal-uncorrelated-independent and @thm-mvn-conditional.
:::

::: {#exr-graphoid-counterexample}
## The need for positivity (starred)
$\star$ The intersection axiom (G5) of @thm-graphoid-axioms can fail without the positivity hypothesis.
Construct a joint distribution of binary $(X,Y,Z,W)$, for instance one in which $X=Y$ deterministically
and $W$ is degenerate, such that $X\perp Y\mid(Z,W)$ and $X\perp W\mid(Z,Y)$ both hold but
$X\perp(Y,W)\mid Z$ fails. Explain precisely which step of a positivity-based proof breaks down.
:::
